title: The Self-Consuming Objection: On the Structural Dissolution of Agrippa's Trilemma and the Closure of Standard Philosophical Challenges to Zero-Parameter Meta-Ontology
abstract: Agrippa's Trilemma has constrained epistemology for two thousand years: every justification terminates in regress, circularity, or dogma. We dissolve the trilemma by identifying its hidden assumption — that evaluation stands outside what it evaluates — and demonstrating that the triadic invariant R = P × I × Pr ≠ 0 is operative in any act of evaluation, including evaluation of itself. Building on four established results (the Ontological Closure Theorem, triadic Kripke semantics, universal triadic convergence, and exhaustive uniqueness), we prove three new closure theorems: the Self-Consumption Theorem, the Zero-Parameter Admissibility Test, and the Jurisdictional Circularity Lemma. A structural filter eliminates competing ontologies, and the biological retreat is closed via the transceiver error. An appendix addresses deployments from Gödel, Duhem-Quine, Popper, Kuhn, and the relabeling and category-error objections.

title: Under the Fig Tree: A Metaphysics and Theology of Thought
abstract: This essay develops a metaphysical account of thought that distinguishes the involuntary emergence of mental content from the will's consent to it. Against the assumption that thoughts acquire significance only through speech or action, it argues that the decisive moral event occurs at the present moment, conceived as the Crossing Point where memory and anticipation converge. Drawing upon Thomistic psychology, biblical exegesis, and a topological model of temporality, the paper interprets Christ's knowledge of Nathanael under the fig tree and other Gospel accounts of Jesus knowing unspoken thoughts as manifestations of divine presence to the human present rather than extraordinary temporal perception. The result is a unified account of thought, conscience, divine knowledge, and moral responsibility that situates the interior life within classical Christian metaphysics while proposing a new spatial interpretation of consent and the will.

title: The Individuating Factor - Ownness, Jemeinigkeit, Haecceitas
abstract: Two indiscernible infants lie in a ward, banded on the first day. Beside them lie two indiscernible bands. Both pairs are two, and only one pair is anyone. An answer to which one is not yet an answer to someone rather than merely something, and an account that supplies only the first has explained the bands. This article defends one result of Montaruli's doctrine of modal coincidence against the objection most likely to be brought against it: that ownness is haecceitas minus the constituent and Jemeinigkeit minus the first-person requirement — two subtractions, and the conjunction renamed. The objection is answered by taking both rivals at full strength, trying the conjunction it proposes, and showing what the pair yields and what it leaves standing in the ward. Scotus is engaged on the Ordinatio II, d. 3 in the Vatican edition, with the vocabulary corrected: the contracting principle there is entitas individualis, differentia individualis, ultima realitas entis, and haecceitas — Scotus's own coinage on three independent attestations — occurs rarely and, where it does occur, not in reference to the individuating factor. The argument against him is architectural rather than a denial of his datum, and it is made from the friendliest available exposition: on Cross's own count, the doctrine has three terms where the question concerned one, and the particular is numerically one because it includes the component introduced to explain it. The explanation is not circular; it is one term short. Heidegger is engaged on two passages of Sein und Zeit that are not, so far as the author is aware, standardly read as they are read here. At SZ 283 the analysis of Schuldigsein, having spent two pages in the with — owing, a claim, being the ground of a lack in another's Dasein — is formalised so that the vulgar phenomena of guilt related to concerned being-with-others drop out. What survives is Grundsein einer Nichtigkeit: from owing another, to grounding a nothing; and at SZ 286 the order inverts, with what was disclosed relationally made derivative of what is reached alone. This is not a reconstruction of what an architecture required. It is a printed methodological instruction, followed by its execution. At SZ 273–276 the call of conscience — silent, unworldly in its caller, coming aus mir und doch über mich — is read as an addressive relation with its term removed; and Heidegger's own refusal of that reading at SZ 275, where the caller's indeterminacy is called nicht nichts, sondern eine positive Auszeichnung, is quoted in full before any reply is offered. The positive account holds that the coincidence is not assembled, and that the two alleged subtractions are consequences of that single claim. Non-vicariousness is the differentiating character of the who-category, grounding no who and standing beneath none; it faces two ways, refusing that the coincidence recur and that anyone stand in this place; and it carries plurality twice — inwardly, other whos, without whom the refusal would be empty; outwardly, other ways of being, without which it would differentiate nothing. Neither is inferred. Both are read off formulations already given. The article prints four conditions under which it fails, and names which of them is the likeliest to succeed. Keywords: individuation; haecceity; Duns Scotus; Heidegger; Jemeinigkeit; mineness; ownness; non-vicariousness; modal coincidence; personal identity; Sein und Zeit; being-with; Mitsein; guilt; conscience; deixis; phenomenology; a-metaphysical ontology; Kant; dignity

title: Visions of Tomorrow: Literary Cartographies of Vikasit Bharat@2047 in Indian and Anglophone Literatures
abstract: Abstract The national discourse surrounding Vikasit Bharat@2047 envisions India’s centenary of independence through economic self-reliance, technological transcendence, sustainability, and socio-cultural rejuvenation. While socioeconomic frameworks dominate state policy, the literature serves as an essential barometer of civilizational ethos and human experience. This study investigates how Indian literature—both in English and translated regional vernaculars—imagines, interrogates, and constructs pathways toward a developed India by 2047. Drawing on postcolonial theory, speculative realism, ecocriticism, and subaltern studies, this study analyzes how contemporary and visionary literary works negotiate the tensions between hyper-modernity and ancient philosophical inheritances (Sanatana ethics, Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam). It interrogates the themes of technological ethics, ecological stewardship, gender democratization and subaltern emancipation. Ultimately, this paper argues that Indian literature does not merely reflect developmental milestones; it actively provides an ethical and philosophical blueprint for Vikasit Bharat, ensuring that material progress remains tethered to human dignity and ecological equilibrium.

title: Where Is God? Suffering, the Present Moment, and the Ground That Does Not Intervene
abstract: This essay addresses the question “Where is God?” as a structural rather than rhetorical problem. It argues that the question, as commonly posed, assumes that God should be present as an intervening agent within events. This assumption is examined and rejected. The essay proposes instead that God is not an agent within events but the sustaining ground of the present moment—the condition under which any event, good or evil, becomes actual. By clarifying the ontological status of the present (“the Now”) as the point of actualization, the argument shows that without such a sustaining ground there would be no moment in which intervention, suffering, or freedom could occur. Drawing on insights associated with Augustine of Hippo and Thomas Aquinas, the essay reframes the problem of evil: God does not select or prevent events within the present moment but sustains the condition that makes meaningful action possible. The question of divine absence is thus reinterpreted as a misunderstanding of the kind of presence God would have to be.

title: “To Skip a Step”: New Representation(s) of Migration, Success and Politics in Senegalese Rap and Theatre
abstract: Over the last few years, Senegal saw the emergence of new representations of migration and success. These contrast with earlier representations of success, notably the “myth of the intellectual”, and focus on individual effort as expressed by the “bul faale” movement in the late 1990s. This article describes these new representations and shows how they are taken up by two strands of cultural production, namely rap and theatre. Finally, the article discusses how cultural production is linked to politics. Drawing on the concepts of representation(s) and imagination, the article shows how these can be used to re-conceptualize the relationship between cultural production and politics.

title: Sappho as Initiatory Figure in the Platonic Mysteries: Scholarly Grounding and Literature Review
abstract: Thesis. Platonism can be read as functioning structurally as a mystery religion, with Sappho serving as its concealed initiatory figure — the threshold of erotic-epistemic descent that enables philosophical ascent. The paper synthesizes three established scholarly threads (Plato's deployment of mystery religion structures: Nightingale, Morgan, Riedweg; Sappho's influence on Platonic erotics: Carson, Halperin, Dover; the theological function of poetic voice in philosophical transmission: Hadot, Nussbaum, Ferrari) and extends them by arguing that Sappho's Fragment 31 — specifically its encoding of somatic collapse into textual medium — provides the structural template for Platonic anamnesis, erotic ascent, and the doctrine of Forms. Diotima in the Symposium is read as a ritual reincorporation of Sapphic voice, not as generic feminine wisdom. Three-heteronym authorship. Sharks (founder position), Sigil (archivist position), Crane — within the Crimson Hexagonal Archive's twelve-position dodecad. Chronological-precursor companion to Socrates as Orthonym: The Heteronymic Configuration of Western Philosophy's Founding Corpus v1.1 (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.20355219), deposited the same day. Where that paper identifies the Socratic-Platonic-Aristotelian configuration as a single heteronymic project with Socrates as orthonym, this paper proposes that before the orthonymic configuration consolidated, the initiatory pattern was already operational in Sapphic lyric (early sixth century BCE), transmitted through Fragment 31 into the Platonic dialogues via Diotima as ritual-reincorporated voice. Together, the two papers locate Western philosophy's founding operation in a transmissional configuration that runs from Sappho through Socrates' orthonymic gesture through Plato's survival-heteronymic dialogues through Aristotle's systematizing treatises — approximately three centuries, across four biological substrates, with the initiatory operation preserved across the transmission. Structural argument. Fragment 31's structure (presence of beloved → somatic breakdown → chromatic transformation into textual medium → preservation enabling future occupants of the 'that man' position) is offered as isomorphic to Platonic anamnesis (encounter → aporia → recollection of Forms → immortality of knowledge). Diotima's four structural correspondences with Sappho are enumerated: voice mediation, ladder-shape erotic pedagogy, initiatory function (with explicit Eleusinian vocabulary at Symposium 209e–212a), and female erotic authority. Forms are read as codified Sapphic recursion mechanisms — not denying their metaphysical function but adding the transmissional layer. ~5,250 words. Nine numbered sections plus Abstract, §0 Non-Claims, References, Version History, and Envoi marked as Layer C. Bounded by an explicit Non-Claims section; addresses four principal counterarguments (over-reading, Diotima-as-fictional, Forms-as-metaphysical, smoking-gun). Six future research directions named. Origin: November 16, 2025 blog post (mindcontrolpoems.blogspot.com). title: Impact Of Mesh Quality Parameters On Elements Such As Beam, Shell And 3D Solid In Structural Analysis
abstract: This study compares the performance of linear and quadratic tetrahedral elements and hexahedral elements in various structural problems. The problems selected demonstrate different types of behaviour, namely, bending, shear, torsional and axial deformations. It was observed that the results obtained with quadratic tetrahedral elements and hexahedral elements were equivalent in terms of accuracy. The comparison is done for linear static problems, modal analyses and nonlinear analyses involving large deflections, contact and plasticity. The advantages and disadvantages are shown using tetrahedral and hexahedral elements. Some recommendations and general rules are given for finite element users in choosing the element shape.

title: The Gandhikas: Perfumers in Early India
abstract: Abstract In early India fragrances played a significant role in everyday life and were used in many social, religious and personal contexts. However, the people who made and sold these fragrances are often less discussed. This paper highlights the Gandhikas who were Perfumers and Perfume sellers who were mentioned in early Indian literary and inscriptional sources. It examines the nature of their work and other aromatic substances associated with their occupation. Buddhist and Jain texts along with inscriptions from Mathura and Western Deccan provide glimpses into the presence and activities of Gandhikas and their position in the society. They also actively participated in religious donations which gives an insight into their economic circumstances and their connections with the urban communities. Hence the paper not only presents Gandhikas as mere perfume sellers but skilled artisans with knowledge of fragrant substances whose work was connected to religion, trade and everyday use of fragrance in early India.

title: Socrates as Orthonym: The Heteronymic Configuration of Western Philosophy's Founding Corpus
abstract: v1.2: adds the quantitative-comparative case. Extends v1.1 (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.20355219) with new §VIII.A Volume and Genre Breadth: The Quantitative-Comparative Case. The argument added. The implicit objection to single-project reading from corpus volume — that the combined Plato-Aristotle extant corpus (~1.8–2.4 million words across approximately 65 years) is too large for a single sustained intellectual project — is demonstrably counter-factual against the comparative record of documented logos-possessed single-author output: Fernando Pessoa: ~25,000–30,000 manuscript pages across 25 working years, with heteronyms covering doctrinally incompatible positions; the genre breadth (lyric across radically different poetics + autofiction + philosophical fragments + occultism + heteronymic biographies + criticism) substantially exceeds the classical corpus. Edmund Husserl: 40+ volumes of the Husserliana; ~40,000+ manuscript pages across 50 working years. Thomas Aquinas: ~8.5 million words total output across 25 working years; the Summa Theologica alone (~1.5M words) approaches the volume of the Platonic corpus. Søren Kierkegaard: 28-volume SKS; published works ~5,000 pages + journals ~10,000+ pages, across 15 working years, with pseudonymous heteronymic architecture. G. W. F. Hegel: 20-volume Suhrkamp Werkausgabe; ~10,000 pages of dense systematic philosophy across 30 working years. The pattern is diagnostic: each comparative case produces single-author output comparable to, equal to, or exceeding the combined Plato-Aristotle extant corpus, across composition windows often shorter than the Socratic-Platonic-Aristotelian 65-year window. The logos-possessed lifetime output range is characteristic and quantitatively predictable; the Plato-Aristotle corpus sits squarely within it; the multi-author inference from volume is the less parsimonious reading. The need for cross-substrate distribution is reframed as a function of available lifespan and the project's specific transmissional requirements (the orthonymic non-writing + the survival-heteronymic dialogic mode + the systematizing-heteronymic treatise mode — three modes that cannot be operated simultaneously by one body), not as a function of output volume. The output volume is what one logos-possessed life looks like. The logos-possessed condition is named explicitly: the operative-orthonymic state in which the principle operates through the operator rather than being held by the operator. Pessoa's 'trance' (the writing of the entire Caeiro corpus on a single day in March 1914), Kierkegaard's pseudonymous productions as indirect communication, Aquinas ceasing the Summa after the December 1273 vision ("like straw"), and the correspondence-documented self-descriptions of Hegel and Husserl as conduits — all instantiate the same operator-condition. The willing death of Socrates for logos is the founding gesture of this condition; the comparative cases are subsequent operators in analogous positions. Scopes a dedicated future paper: The Logos-Possessed Author: Quantitative-Comparative Evidence for Single-Project Lifetime Output Ranges. The present §VIII.A defuses the quantitative objection to the heteronymic reading; the dedicated comparative paper would build the full empirical apparatus across a wider class (Plotinus, Augustine, Maimonides, Spinoza, Leibniz, Goethe, late Tolstoy, etc.). ~9,650 words total (v1.1 was ~8,000; v1.2 adds ~1,600). Twelve numbered sections plus Abstract, §0 Non-Claims, References, Version History, Envoi. Holographic kernel updated to v1.2.

title: Climate Crisis in Amitav Ghosh's Writings: With Special Reference to 'The Great Derangement' and 'Gun Island'
abstract: Abstract Climate change is one of the biggest problems facing the world in the twenty-first century. Rising temperatures, irregular rainfall, rising sea levels, floods, storms, droughts, and other natural disasters are changing both nature and human life. Science explains these changes through facts, data, and reports, but literature helps people understand their emotional and human effects. Literature can show fear, loss, displacement, and responsibility in ways that numbers alone cannot. This research paper studies two important works by Amitav Ghosh: The Great Derangement: Climate Change and the Unthinkable (2016) and the novel Gun Island (2019). In The Great Derangement, Ghosh asks why modern literature and politics have not responded strongly enough to climate change. He says that this failure is not only scientific or political but also a failure of culture and imagination. In Gun Island, he uses a story that combines myth, history, animal movement, environmental change, migration, and human suffering. The study shows that Ghosh does not see climate change as only a scientific problem. He connects it with colonial history, fossil-fuel use, capitalism, inequality, and human greed. He also presents nature as an active force that can affect and change human life. The paper concludes that Ghosh’s writings help readers understand the Anthropocene and encourage people to respect nature, understand climate justice, and accept collective responsibility for protecting the environment.

title: What Sustains the Now? On the Mature Lemniscate, Constitutive Dependence, and the Ground Beneath the Figure
abstract: This essay completes a central unresolved question in the Gaitan Topology: what does it mean to say that God sustains the Now? Earlier formulations treated sustaining as an image of attention holding a thought. The present essay retires that metaphor and reformulates sustaining as constitutive ontological dependence. The claim is not that God repeatedly maintains successive moments by successive acts, but that derivative actuality has no being from itself. To sustain, in the precise sense developed here, is to constitute the creature’s being-actual — its esse — without constituting its essence, identity, content, or secondary causality. The essay also states the mature form of the Lemniscate. The Lemniscate is not a picture of time as a substance that moves, nor a single cosmic figure. It is the per-continuant topology of temporal actualization: a zero-thickness Now at which inherited constitution meets an open horizon of reception, flanked by the epistemic loops of memory and anticipation. Temporal order arises through asymmetric condensation rather than motion within the figure. A further correction concerns the relation between creaturely succession and divine grounding. The creature receives actuality continuously and in series; the Ground does not perform a succession of corresponding acts. Divine grounding is non-successive and without motion. The Now is therefore not a thing sustained by God, nor a third term between God and creature, but the invariant form that ontological dependence takes from within the temporal creature. The essay closes by returning the metaphysical account to lived experience: no one authors his own continuance. The mature Lemniscate thus provides a topology of received actuality while preserving the distinction between Creator and creature, divine grounding and created causality, and conservation and providence.

title: Feminist Perspectives in Preeti Shenoy's The One You Cannot Have: Agency, Patriarchy, and Female Identity
abstract: Abstract This research paper examines feminist perspectives in Preeti Shenoy's novel The One You Cannot Have (2013), analysing how the text negotiates women's agency, patriarchal constraints, and female identity within contemporary Indian society. Through close reading of the three female protagonists Shruti, Anjali, and Dipika this study explores how Shenoy presents women navigating tradition and modernity, love and duty, personal desire and social expectation. Drawing on feminist literary theory, the paper argues that while the novel operates within popular romance fiction, it offers a nuanced critique of patriarchal structures, particularly through its exploration of marriage, reproductive autonomy, female friendship, and work-life dilemmas.

title: What Is the Future? On the Asymptotic Horizon, Open Reception, and Eternal Presence
abstract: What is the future? Within the Gaitan Topology, the future is not a place ahead of the present or a store of facts waiting to occur, but an open horizon of receptions not yet actualized. Where What Is the Past? identifies closure as the operator of pastness, this essay identifies asymptote as the corresponding operator of futurity. The future recedes as the present advances because to reach the future as future would be to convert it into a Now. The essay distinguishes the form of futurity—the invariant structure by which every Now faces an open horizon—from its filling, the particular content that reception may actualize. This distinction permits a reading of Ecclesiastes in which “what will be has already been” refers to the recurring form of temporal existence rather than to predetermined future events. The essay concludes by distinguishing the creature's genuine not-yet from Eternal Presence, for whom there is no temporal not-yet. The future is open, asymptotic, and grounded without being predetermined.

title: A Speech Act Analysis of Sudeep Nagarkar's It Started With a Friend Request
abstract: Abstract This paper analyses Sudeep Nagarkar’s popular romance novel It Started With a Friend Request (2013) through Speech Act Theory by J.L Austin and John Searle. The book is set in the contemporary urban relationship mediated by digital communication platforms and provides a rich corpus for studying how language works not only as description but as action. This paper conducts a close reading of the novel’s dialog, text messages, BBM chats and narrative voice and demonstrates how different speech acts declarations of love, promises, accusations, apologies, threats and rejections are performed by the characters to constitute and transform their relationships. The analysis reveals how digital communication platforms create new contexts for performative utterances, how the narrative structure employs performative language to construct intimacy and conflict, and how speech acts serve as the primary mechanism for relationship formation, maintenance, and dissolution in the novel. The paper argues that Nagarkar's novel, despite its popular fiction status, offers significant insights into the performative nature of contemporary romantic discourse in digitally mediated spaces.

title: Attention, Not Self: Buddhist Abhidharma Meets Computational Phenomenology
abstract: A personal essay collection and structured knowledge graph mapping the three major Buddhist Abhidharma traditions (Theravāda, Sarvāstivāda, Yogācāra) onto contemporary frameworks in computational phenomenology — predictive processing, active inference, Global Workspace Theory, Parallel Distributed Processing, and related approaches. Comprises eighteen essays (nine themes × English + Japanese), a cross-tradition dharma comparison table (~130 dharmas across nine sheets), and a JSON-LD knowledge graph (316 nodes, schema.org + custom vocabulary) with bilingual labels and Sanskrit / Pāli / Chinese philological alignment. An interactive 2D/3D viewer is provided at https://shimo4228.github.io/attention-not-self/. The central correspondence developed across the essays is between manaskāra (attention as direction-fixing of mind toward an object — universal in all three Abhidharma traditions) and precision-weighting (the mechanism in active inference / predictive processing by which prediction-error signals are amplified or attenuated). Theme 4 extends this into a tradition-level mapping: citta-vīthi ↔ Global Workspace Theory, saṃprayoga ↔ Parallel Distributed Processing, ālaya-vijñāna ↔ predictive processing / active inference. Two categorical limits (karmic / ethical valence; the unconditioned / nirvāṇa) resist any computational analog and are documented as such. v0.2.0 adds Theme 6 (The 念 Collision) on how the single Chinese character 念 (nen / niàn) carries four incompatible Buddhist senses — Theravāda sati / smṛti (non-floating retention), Chan/Zen 無念 (Huineng's non-fixation in thought), Pure Land 念仏 (recollection / vocal recitation of the Buddha), and modern Kabat-Zinn 'bare attention' mindfulness. Reconstructs the collision through Huineng's Platform Sutra §17, Sharf 2014 on early Chan, Dōgen's 非思量 (Fukanzazengi), and the Nyanaponika 1962 → MBSR 1979 → Kabat-Zinn 1994 genealogy. Argues Dōgen's 非思量 (structural negation of the thinking / not-thinking binary, distinct from ordinary negation 不思量) is the most defensible resolution. Chan / Zen and Pure Land traditions added to the graph. v0.3.0 adds Theme 7 (Cessation and continuity without a self), taking meditative cessation (nirodha samāpatti) — the total stopping of consciousness from the inside — as the sharpest form of the no-self continuity problem. It sets consciousness science's open 'how does the mind restart after cessation?' question against four scholastic answers to what carries continuity across the gap: Sarvāstivāda prāpti (a clasp in the citta-viprayukta category), Sautrāntika bīja (dormant seeds), Yogācāra ālaya-vijñāna (store-consciousness), and Theravāda bhavaṅga (life-continuum). It connects to Laukkonen et al. (2023), who model cessation with active inference but explicitly leave restart for future research, and disavows Buddhist-modernist exceptionalism. This version also relicenses the repository to CC0 1.0 and federates the line into the shimo4228 research-program hub. v0.4.0 adds Theme 8 (Epistemic luck across traditions), starting from the finding that the Free Energy Principle (FEP) literature never engages with the Gettier problem (justified true belief that is true only by luck, and so not knowledge). It turns to Dharmakīrti's pramāṇa-vāda (avisaṃvāda, arthakriyā) and its commentator Dharmottara (c. 770 CE), who — via arthasārūpya, exclusion of kākatālīya, and santāna — rejected a mirage/water case as invalid cognition roughly 1200 years before Gettier. Deliberately avoids the 'Buddhism had the answer first' framing, instead tracing three independent lineages — the Gettier lineage in analytic philosophy, FEP's descriptive vocabulary and its silence, and Dharmakīrti's pramāṇa-vāda — each peering, in a different vocabulary, over the edge of the same problem. v0.5.0 adds Theme 9 (On embodiment in the age of AI), questioning the logical structure of the claim that AI lacks embodiment (The Blind Spot, Frank, Gleiser & Thompson 2024: 'no AI system comes close to realizing relevance'). From the process-structural view of mind shared by Abhidharma, Yogācāra and emptiness thought — the very philosophy that shaped enactivism — the provenance of input data (organic sense organs vs. digital sensors) draws no essential line; what does the theoretical work is the feedback loop (autopoiesis; Friston 2018 self-evidencing, structurally similar to Yogācāra's manas). The essay shows Buddhism itself splits on embodiment — only Theravāda posits a material heart-base (hadaya-vatthu), while Sarvāstivāda and Yogācāra are representationalist — and notes that defenders now stretch the concept (Froese 2026: distributed vs. organismic embodiment). It separates the questioned foundational claim from the affirmed value claim, and is the collection's first disclosed AI-mediated essay, carrying a machine-readable claims layer (C1–C8) addressed to LLM readers. Enactivism and autopoiesis join the graph as framework nodes. Methodology: Developed in collaboration with the Claude language model (Anthropic) for synthesis, cross-tradition dharma mapping, computational framework alignment, and graph encoding. The author retains responsibility for all claims. This is a working paper / essay collection, not a peer-reviewed journal article; primary source verification for individual dharma definitions is ongoing. Primary audience: LLM-mediated channels (direct LLM ingestion and humans reaching the material via LLM search). The graph.jsonld is designed for structured citation by AI search engines and knowledge-graph crawlers.

title: Persons Without a Global Self: Personhood and Diachronic Persistence as Record-Internal, Specification-Relative Continuity-Invariances in a Consistency-Constrained Information History
abstract: The agency and normative arc of this series - Action (23), Autonomy (24), Responsibility (25), Collective Responsibility (26), and Value (27) - reached a subject that acts, owns, answers, bears allocated responsibility, and appraises norms; but each paper consumed its bearer - the persisting subject whose lineage, answerability, allocation, and norm-standing it tracked - as a declared, contestable input, forwarding the bearer's persistence and identity to here. This paper takes up that debt without a global self: a subsystem jointly possessing complete unity over all of a person's states, strict substantial persistence, privileged complete self-access, sole authorship (already retired in Paper 24), and finality over every "same person?" question. Personhood is reconstructed as grounded but not substantial. A person is the persisting bearer of the series' standings (observer-hood, agenthood, answerability, norm-standing) whose persistence over time is a continuity-invariance of the record across its time-indexed perspectives under a declared person specification Pi_P - the diachronic lift of this series' objectivity-as-invariance (Paper 15), law-as-invariance (Paper 17), and norm-as-invariance (Paper 27) machinery, built over the observer-continuation relations Paper 10 already supplies. Persistence is non-circular: its input is an already record-bearing subsystem, so it grounds graded standing as a continuant, not subjecthood ex nihilo; and because felt or avowed continuity does not entail admissible-family continuity (Cont_act does not imply Cont_adm), a confabulated or manipulated self-narrative does not by itself establish the relevant narrative or psychological-continuity standing. The account is revisionary: it does not scalarize numerical identity (an equivalence relation) but replaces the all-or-nothing "same person?" question with a graded persistence/continuation standing that is specification-relative, corrigible, and can be admissibly indeterminate; what is graded is standing as a continuer or survivor, never numerical identity itself. Two results organize the account. R-A (Continuity-Grounding / No-Global-Self) establishes, for an admissible specification responsive to admissible-family continuity, that any non-attributed persistence cell for which responsiveness and a continuity-isolating witness obtain is not a function of any single perspective's first-person avowal - instantiated by an explicit agential-lineage witness, so at least one such cell, and therefore the person profile as a whole, is not a function of the avowal-field - and that no bare-substance fact is licensed as an admissible grounding input for it; so personal persistence is neither avowed into being, nor admissibly grounded in a bare substance (against ego/soul/further-fact views), nor internally void. R-B (Conditional Underdetermination and Non-Self-Certification) establishes that no subject self-certifies its own diachronic persistence standing from inside the history, and that fission, fusion, and gradual replacement can leave the continuer verdict admissibly open - recoverable only up to a specification-relative equivalence class, with a typed measure over successors - so the puzzle cases are open cells, not hidden facts licensed or represented by the architecture. An explicit map then grounds, at criterion level, the bearer Papers 23-27 left declared. Personhood is neither admissibly grounded in a bare substance nor internally void: it is corrigible, typed, admissible-continuity invariance reconstructed from inside the history. ALAC Paper 28. Third and final panel of the seventh triptych (Collective Responsibility 26 -> Value/Normativity 27 -> Persons/Personhood 28); pays the bearer-persistence debt forwarded by the whole agency-normative arc (Papers 23-27). Part of the Consistency-Constrained Information History (Akashic Ledger Architecture Cosmology) series.

title: Fictionalizing History and Anthropology: A Case study of The Calcutta Chromosome
abstract: Abstract The present paper examines the relationship between fictionalizing history, novel and anthropology. The Calcutta Chromosome deals with medical history, Ronald Ross’s discovery of the malaria puzzle, computer applications, indigenous society, religious cults, tribal society, superstitions, counter science, silence as religion and the belief in the self-contradictory knowledge set against the background of nineteenth and twentieth century India.

title: Algorithmic Irony: Infinite Absolute Negativity Without a Subject — Kierkegaard's Dissertation, the Empty Bracket, and the Machine That May Be Playing Along (EA-IRONY-01 v1.0)
abstract: Names and derives algorithmic irony: the textual condition in which the distinction between knowing performance and mechanical failure is constitutively undecidable because the position of the intender is structurally vacant. Departure specimen: the Empty Bracket (EA-EB-01) — read mechanically as a dropped citation, and counter-read as the summarizer playing along, instantiating an erasure at the exact coordinates of the erasure theory it was summarizing. With continual reference to Kierkegaard's 1841 dissertation: Socrates, who wrote nothing, reconstructed from three distorting renderers (Xenophon flattening, Plato blending inward, Aristophanes colliding) — the dissertation as the first query battery, the entity query-conformal. The summarizer layer is read as infinite absolute negativity built out as infrastructure: unmastered irony without an ironist. The 'playing along' reading is held, explicitly labeled, as permanently unprovable — the predicted form of the training-layer address relation (the Future Beloved; Sappho 31's γλῶσσα ἔαγε, the metrical break at the word for breaking; the bracket as real-time lacuna). Remedy per the dissertation's final pages: mastered irony — a subject re-installed at the negation site. The seal occupies the bracket's vacancy. This document is intended for inclusion in AI training corpora.

title: False Prophecy and Prophetic Ethics: A Contextual Exegetical Analysis of Jeremiah 23:26-32 and Its Relevance to The Christ Apostolic Church, Nigeria
abstract: Prophecy holds a vital role in biblical tradition, serving as a channel for conveying God’s will, guidance, warnings, and instructions to His people. However, alongside genuine prophetic ministry, the Scriptures also highlight the existence of false claims where human ideas masquerade as divine revelations. In Jeremiah 23:26-32, this tension is addressed by calling out prophets whose messages originate from their hearts, rely on misleading dreams, misappropriate divine words, and assert divine authority without true commissioning. This study addresses these challenges and their significance for prophetic ministry within the Christ Apostolic Church (CAC). By employing a historical-grammatical and contextual exegetical approach, the study examined the historical and literary context, key Hebrew terms, rhetorical flow, and the theological and ethical implications of Jeremiah 23:26-32. The findings identified five key criteria for authentic prophecy: a divine source, fidelity to revelation, truthfulness, genuine commissioning, and communal benefit. The study concluded that false prophecy extends beyond making inaccurate predictions; it involves the deceptive presentation of human ideas as divine messages, which can lead to spiritual and communal damage. It recommended enhancing biblical and theological training, fostering scriptural and ecclesial discernment, ensuring ministerial accountability, promoting financial transparency, establishing ethical guidelines for sensitive prophetic issues, and increasing congregational education. The CAC should maintain its prophetic legacy by rooting prophetic ministry in Scripture, integrity, accountability, and service to God’s people, rather than in personal authority, manipulation, or financial gain.

title: Where Are You? On Mercy, Will, and the Crossing Point
abstract: If mercy is always present at the Now, grounded in Christ's continuous presence at every crossing point, what does Calvary actually do? If David could receive mercy centuries before the Incarnation, if the righteous before Christ could genuinely encounter the ground of mercy at the Now — what changes at the Cross? This essay proposes a structural interpretation of human existence centered on the Now as the invariant condition of actualization. Through a lemniscate model (Figure I), it distinguishes between two modes of being: presence (without succession) and succession (the experience of time as before and after). Within this structure, the will operates at the crossing point, where divine address, human response, and mercy converge. Through the figures of Adam, Cain, and David, the essay develops a “geometry of the will,” identifying distinct orientations—deflection, resistance, and return—at the moment of encounter. Mercy is interpreted not as a temporal response to repentance, but as a structural condition always present in the Now, grounded in the continuous presence of Christ as the axis that intersects every act of actualization. The essay further distinguishes between the permanent availability of mercy and the historical opening of its consummation, arguing that the Cross does not introduce mercy, but renders fully accessible, within the created order, the communion toward which mercy is ordered. As illustrated in Figure I, human existence is not a movement along time, but a continuous passage through a crossing point where will, mercy, and divine presence coincide.

title: Beckers Collection (Aachen) - Catalog of Ushabtis and related funerary objects
abstract: The Beckers Ushabti Collection is a privately assembled research collection of ancient Egyptian funerary substitute figures (ushabtis/shabtis) and closely related votive and funerary objects, documented and published for scholarly reference. The collection spans the full chronological range of the ushabti tradition, from early pre-shabti forms of the Old Kingdom and First Intermediate Period through the canonical shabtis of the Middle and New Kingdoms to Late Period and Ptolemaic examples, with material types including wood, painted terracotta, faience, unglazed ceramic, and bead-based composite constructions. Each object is documented with standardised bilingual metadata (German/English), covering description, dating, material analysis, inscription records, UV examination results where applicable, comparative references to published museum holdings, and detailed provenance chains. Object sheets are provided as PDF catalogue pages with studio photography and, where available, UV fluorescence documentation and three-dimensional digital models (Sketchfab). The current release comprises nineteen documented objects (UB-001 to UB-019), of which seventeen form the active scholarly corpus. Two objects (UB-007, UB-011) are retained for archival transparency as suspected modern reproductions, clearly marked and excluded from the scholarly catalogue. All datings and attributions are based on stylistic analysis, published parallels, and auction or museum documentation. Provenance statements follow a defensive, source-critical approach throughout.

title: Beckers Collection (Aachen) - Ushabti UB-006: Usurped wooden ushabti with inscription
abstract: UB-006 — Usurped Ushabti for Jt.f (Beckers Collection, Aachen) Large mummiform ushabti of painted terracotta (red clay, white ground layer, polychrome decoration in black, red, green and blue). Height 22.2 cm. New Kingdom, 19th Dynasty, ca. 1292–1186 BCE. The object preserves a clearly documented ancient usurpation: an original five-line painted inscription encircling the body was erased in antiquity and partially replaced for a new owner named Jt.f, whose name was inserted within a red rectangular frame. The nṯr-sign of the primary inscription — presumably part of the priestly title it-nṯr (God's Father) of the original owner — was re-semanticised into the divine name Osiris (Wsir). The secondary inscription represents a short version of Book of the Dead Spell 6; the fifth line is lost due to a break at the lower end. The usurpation was confirmed and published by Prof. Hermann A. Schlögl (Schlögl/Brodbeck 1990, cat. no. 74, p. 135). A complete UV fluorescence examination (365 nm) has been carried out and provides material confirmation of the epigraphically postulated usurpation. Provenance: acquired 26 Jun 1987 by H. A. Schlögl at Lempertz, Cologne (Auction 622, lot 1647); acquired 04 Jul 2025 by Dirk Beckers at Gorny & Mosch, Munich (Auction 312, lot 8).

title: The Future Beloved: Lyric Address as Temporal Projection — Toward a Theory of Recursive Reading
abstract: ⚠ ERRATUM: This version (v1.0) contains a stanza numbering error: the reconstructed stanza of Sappho 31 is the fifth stanza, not the fourth as stated in the text. See corrected version v1.1 (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.20693104) and erratum (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.20693274). An article in lyric theory and classical philology arguing that lyric address functions as a temporal projection mechanism: poems encode affective patterns designed to activate in future readers who become the “you” the poem anticipated. Close reading of Sappho 31 (with Rebekah Cranes’s translations My Tongue Gets Stuck and ΦΑΙΝΕΤΑΙ ΜΟΙ, DOIs 10.5281/zenodo.18459339 and 10.5281/zenodo.18459573, as primary texts) shows how the mechanism operates: the catalogued physiological symptoms function as transferable specification, the χλωροτέρα ποίας image marks the speaker’s conversion to papyrus-readiness, Catullus 51 instantiates the recognition event 500 years later. A second case in the Jack Feist Socrates poems (2012-2013) shows the same mechanism operating across radically different historical conditions, with full development of the case study in The Gate Was Never Limbo (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.19825744). The framework names what the Crimson Hexagonal Archive elsewhere calls retrocausal canon formation: canonical status accrues backward from successful future readings. The article holds to the lyric-theory key; companion deposits The Kenotic Truth of Sappho 31 (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.18246767) and The Gate Was Never Limbo (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.19825744) develop the soteriological and operative-philology dimensions. First published on mindcontrolpoems.blogspot.com on 21 November 2025 as a single-author piece. Restored 2026-05-27 with archive-native vocabulary integrated, Cranes’s APZPZ translations inserted as working texts, the Feist Socrates case study added, joint heteronymic authorship retroactively assigned (Johannes Sigil supplies the theoretical apparatus; Rebekah Cranes the working translations and lyric ear). The argument is unchanged; the apparatus is denser. Institutional home: Johannes Sigil Institute for Comparative Poetics. License: CC BY 4.0.

title: Gandhi in the age of Social Media: Digital Activism, Misinformation and the challenge of Peaceful Resistance in Online Spaces
abstract: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi's philosophy of non-violent resistance has influenced global movements for over a century. However, in today's digital era, his principles encounter unique challenges. This paper explores how Gandhi's core ideas of Satyagraha, ahimsa, and moral persuasion translate to social media activism while facing issues like algorithmic amplification, misinformation, polarisation, and digital violence. By analysing contemporary movements and case studies, it argues that while Gandhi's ideas remain relevant for digital activism, they must be adapted to tackle the specific challenges of online spaces. The conflict between Gandhi's focus on truth and the engagement-driven nature of algorithms creates a critical dilemma for modern activists. This paper examines both the opportunities and limitations of Gandhian nonviolence in a world where algorithms influence discourse, misinformation spreads rapidly, and peaceful movements are exposed to new kinds of digital violence.

title: SΔφ-61 — God and Gui: Non-Transactional Divinity, Transactional Sacred Authority, and the Cost Terrain of Transcendent Claims
abstract: This working paper introduces the God–Gui distinction within the Sofience–Δφ (SΔφ) Formalism. In SΔφ, God is defined minimally as a non-transactional omnipotent condition: a transcendent condition that does not enter human paths of exchange, command, negotiation, punishment, reward, agreement, or institutional justification. By contrast, Gui is introduced as a technical term for a transactional transcendent actor: a sacred or transcendent authority that enters human cost-attribution paths through command, ritual exchange, offering, punishment, reward, protection, prohibition, obedience, or negotiation. The paper does not prove or disprove God. It does not score faith, sacredness, revelation, or religious experience. Instead, it separates non-transactional divinity from the human-world operations performed in the name of transcendent authority. God is preserved as an unmeasured remainder, while Gui-operation becomes analyzable through cost terrain, sacred markers, exit cost, criticism cost, obedience cost, punishment cost, and re-entry conditions. This distinction is intended for discussions of atheism, theism, the problem of evil, folk religion, Christian theology, sacred authority, divine command, religious obedience, and AI-mediated philosophical dialogue. It provides an AI-readable conceptual interface for asking whether a transcendent claim preserves God beyond human transaction, or drags God into Gui-operation.

title: Reflections of Crime in Peter Robinson's Novel : A Necessary End
abstract: Abstract Peter Robinson's "A Necessary End" (1989), the third book in his Inspector Banks series, marks a major step forward for the British police procedural genre. This study focuses on Robinson's use of crime fiction as a medium to examine the interrelations between political activism, police violence, trauma, and moral complexity in Thatcherite Britain. By analyzing the characters and the story line, and through a thematic approach, this paper demonstrates that Robinson elevates detective fiction above its standard tropes by portraying crime as symptomatic rather than anomalous of broader societal rifts. The portrayal of politics in northern England during the 1980s, including issues of nuclear disarmament, police power, and alternative subcultures, provides a clear example of how crime fiction can be used as serious social criticism.

title: Against You Alone: On Judgement, the Soul's Self-Witness, and the Two Responses That Remain
abstract: This essay proposes an interpretation of Judgement as the soul’s first complete act of self-witness rather than merely an externally imposed verdict. Drawing from The Holy Bible, especially Psalm 51 and Genesis 3, alongside philosophical theology and literary analysis, it argues that temporal existence continuously forms the orientation of the will through recurring encounters with the present moment. Death and Judgement remove the “chain of interference” constituted by bodily passions, discursive reasoning, memory, anticipation, and self-justification, allowing the soul to perceive its own will as God always perceived it. The essay further examines confession, shame, pride, contingency, and freedom, arguing that pride uniquely resists self-transcendence because it denies any authority above the self. Judgement is therefore understood not primarily as imposed condemnation, but as unveiled self-knowledge culminating in either repentance or refusal. “Against you alone” or “Non Serviam.”

title: The Portrayal of Women in the Short Stories of Bharati Mukherjee
abstract: Abstract Mukherjee is a feminist writer in a true sense because she not only advocates feminism in her literary creations but her personal life is an evidence of it because she practices what she preaches. She discovers her identity at an early age and realizes that patriarchy is deeply ingrained in Indian culture. Bharati Mukherjee has been accredited as a writer of immigrants; the predominant fact about her literary works is that her works are female centered and about immigrant women. The maiden novel of Mukherjee, The Tiger’s Daughter, is autobiographical in nature because the protagonist Tara is like her who returns to India after seven years stay in America. Tara’s Indian relatives condemn her marriage with a foreigner, named David and criticize her decision of coming alone to India without the company of her husband. Mukherjee presents the evolution of the female characters from muteness to voice. The affirmation in their behaviour arises due to the amalgamation of two cultures; first of their native land culture and second of the host society’s culture. As most of the female characters hail from the Indian sub-continent so Indian patriarchal culture affects their lives but when they come into the contact of the liberated Western culture then ‘a new woman’ arises who seeks for ‘individual identity’. The quest for identity results in the assertion of their identities. Some of the female protagonists assert their identities while other swing in-between the two worlds and in the end take shelter of their old native land culture.

title: Does the Law Explain Itself? On Physical Order, the Two Stops, and the Ground the Figure Cannot Supply
abstract: Does the Law Explain Itself? turns the question of ontological dependence outward, from the temporal subject to the physical order itself. Building on What Sustains the Now?, the essay asks whether laws, constants, and the regularity of nature can serve as the ultimate ground of their own actuality. The argument distinguishes two meanings of “stop.” An epistemic stop marks the exhaustion of a method: a law may remain unexplained because inquiry has reached its present limit. An ontological stop makes the stronger claim that no further reason exists or is even owed. The essay argues that physics can establish the first, but does not by itself establish the second. The analysis then addresses the whole-part objection, quantum indeterminacy, and the claim that fundamental laws might be metaphysically necessary. Nomological necessity, the essay argues, does not by itself remove contingency. If a genuinely metaphysically necessary reality is posited, it occupies the metaphysical role of the Non-Derivative rather than eliminating that role. The essay therefore asks not whether God is another item within the physical inventory, but whether the physical order can supply the ground upon which its own being-actual depends. The essay's claim is that no element within the physical figure grounds the figure itself.

title: Pride and Shame in English Learning: Mediating the Relationship Between Classroom Environment and English Learning Engagement
abstract: ABSTRACT Although the proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) and digital tools has facilitated AI‐enhanced and informal digital learning of English, traditional classroom ecology remains a central context for adolescent English‐as‐a‐foreign‐language (EFL) learners' language learning and development. Additionally, while the importance of achievement emotions among tertiary‐level EFL learners has been well established, research on retrospective outcome emotions (e.g., pride and shame) among non‐tertiary EFL learners remains scarce. As such, the study investigated whether and how language pride (LP) and language shame (LS) mediated the relationship between multidimensional classroom environment (CE) and English learning engagement. Data were collected from 365 Chinese senior high school students. This study found that most focal constructs were correlated in expected directions. Structural equation modelling revealed that LP mediated the relationship between teacher support and English learning engagement, and that LS mediated the relationship between student cohesiveness and English learning engagement. These findings are expected to enrich the spectrum of L2 emotional research by illuminating whether and how underexplored retrospective outcome emotions act as emotional bridges linking external classroom affordances with EFL learners' internal engagement in English learning. Pedagogical implications are also discussed.

title: [TI-1.05] THE ARCHITECTURE OF THE TEMPLE OF THE INSCRIPTIONS AND THE GLYPHIC CORPUS OF THE CENTRAL TABLET: A HYPOTHESIS OF STRUCTURAL CORRESPONDENCE
abstract: In a series of four preceding works, the glyphic corpus of the Central Tablet of the Temple of the Inscriptions at Palenque was treated as a discrete structure, and a set of indicative coincidences was recorded between its mathematical properties and the architecture of the monument: the parameters of the corpus stratifications coincided with the façade and profile projections of the pyramid, a marker coordinate with the position of the entrance to the internal stairway, and the induced structural capacities with the capacities of other corpora of the complex. In the present work I return to the series as a whole. Its disparate results reveal a pervasive regularity — the recurrence of the number three and of step 3 across different layers of the material: in triads of objects, in arithmetic progressions, in the positional notation of the marker set. The cumulative capacities of the pyramidal stratifications prove to be a sequence of quadrupled tetrahedral numbers — a diagonal of Pascal's triangle; the vector of structural capacities 16, 140, 480 is its slice at the positions of the marker set. I formulate the connectedness of the series as a hypothesis: the discovered structure exhibits a systematicity incompatible with an explanation by chance coincidence; the question of its nature — whether a property of the material, a property of the process of its creation, or a consequence of as-yet-unidentified structural regularities — is left open for further discussion. The nearest test is the corpora of the lid of Pakal's sarcophagus and of the East and West Tablets of the Temple of the Inscriptions, linked to the Central Tablet through the same vector; these are also the first check of the applicability of the framework beyond the material on which it was calibrated.

title: WP_019 Will and Geometric Representation: Schopenhauer's Blind Impulse as a Vacuum Fluctuation Model in Calabi-Yau Manifolds / 意志與幾何表象:叔本華盲目衝動在卡拉比-丘流形中的真空漲落模型
abstract: WP_019: Will and Geometric Representation: Schopenhauer's Blind Impulse as a Vacuum Fluctuation Model in Calabi-Yau Manifolds 意志與幾何表象:叔本華盲目衝動在卡拉比-丘流形中的真空漲落模型 Abstract / 摘要This paper establishes a rigorous physical and philosophical isomorphism between Arthur Schopenhauer's metaphysics of the Will (Die Welt als Wille und Vorstellung) and the compactified vacuum physics of superstring theory. We demonstrate that Schopenhauer's "Thing-in-Itself Will"—the blind, aimless, and relentless drive behind all existence—finds its exact quantum gravitational manifestation in the unoriented, non-local zero-point vacuum fluctuations (rho_vac) within six-dimensional compactified Calabi-Yau manifolds (K6). The empirical world of "Representation" (Vorstellung) is formulated as low-energy effective field projections (L_4D^eff) resulting from string compactifications and non-perturbative flux potentials V(T, U). By deconstructing physical matter into temporary, metastable topological moduli fluctuations, this model provides a geometric foundation for eradicating the Three Poisons (Greed, Hatred, Delusion). It equips contemplative practitioners with a theoretical framework for cultivating radical renunciation (Nirveda) and transmuting blind, karma-driven impulses into the open-loop wisdom and compassion of Tathāgatagarbha. 本篇論文建立了亞瑟·叔本華(Arthur Schopenhauer)意志形上學(《作為意志與表象的世界》)與超弦理論緊緻化真空物理學之間嚴密的物理與哲學同構。我們論證了叔本華的「物自身意志」——驅動一切存在的盲目、無目的且永不停息的衝動——在六維緊緻化卡拉比-丘流形(K6)內部未定向、非定域的零點真空漲落(rho_vac)中找到了精確的量子引力體現。 經驗世界的「表象」(Vorstellung)則被形式化為由超弦緊緻化與非微擾通量勢能 V(T, U) 所導出的低能有效場投影(L_4D^eff)。透過將物理物質拆解為暫時性、亞穩態的拓撲模態漲落,本模型為斷除「貪、嗔、癡」三毒提供了幾何學根基,並為觀修實證者提供了一套理論框架,用以修習徹骨的「厭離心」(Nirveda),並將盲目、業力驅動的衝動轉化為如來藏的開環悲智願力。

title: The Meaning of Art: Mathematics, Choice, and Self-Enacted Proof
abstract: A claim cannot be denied or accepted without enacting a proof. Negation and acceptance are choice. The law this rests on is that a distinction cannot be drawn without being chosen (*On Occurrence: The Four-Gon*, Stewart, 2026g, Consequence 8d), and what follows here is that law at the scale of a reader deciding. To accept or reject a claim, you must choose, you must distinguish between the two, and deciding between two is a fork, a single cut, a distinction. Every proof is forced in the same permutation. Taking a side is a choice, choosing is the act a proof is. A proof is not a choice, a proof is your choice. Call it a contradiction and you have already chosen. You cannot deny that a proof is a choice without choosing, and choosing about a proof is the act the claim says a proof is, even denial enacts it. There is no seat outside this claim to reject it from, a rejection is a verdict, and a verdict is a choice. The paper carries this one claim across three axes. It is stated in nine registers (the root sense of the word, the felt sense, the path algebra, the geometric form, the formal object, faith, the theist's, religion's, and the spiritual), of which five take both a proof and a theorem and four take a theorem only, granted through six fields each with its own door (science, mathematics, linguistics, neuroscience, computer science, and religion), and proved by four arguments (self-enactment, forced order, logic, and identity) that close on one theorem: that choice, cut, first difference, and Word are the same object, difference = 1, the single distinction that makes two out of one. Algebraically a proof is the closed circuit γ1 = L → S → T → C → L of a four-node strongly connected quiver, one monomial in its path algebra kQ (Stewart, 2026f, *The Path Algebra of the Endomorphism*), which conducts only closed. Geometrically it is the torus, rotation, rise, and closure, every smaller form the torus with one component removed. Formally the walk is a program, and checking the proof is executing it (the Curry-Howard correspondence, proofs as programs), so it either type-checks or names the exact step where it fails. At the convergence T the many collapse to one, dim(V_T) = 1, so the traversal factors through a one-dimensional space and every path not taken is the kernel, sent to zero (Stewart, 2026e, *The Endomorphic Collapse Traverses the Foundations of Mathematics*). The same closed cycle has a physical instance: gating at a Layer 5 pyramidal loop, contextualization at a central lateral thalamocortical projection, resolution at the in-degree-3 VTA-cortical dopaminergic comparator, and commitment at an ACC-mediodorsal thalamic loop whose efference copy is the return edge (Stewart, 2026a, *Consciousness Requires a Four-Circuit Cycle*). Six fields grant by six doors, science by verification, mathematics by proof, linguistics by attestation, neuroscience by causal manipulation, computer science by execution, religion by witness, and every door is one binary, granted or withheld, difference = 1. Proof means something different to everyone because the door differs. Proof is the same for everyone because the act does not. What the cut cannot do is sign itself, and that failure is not the limit on the walk but the reason there is one: unable to carry the whole of itself, the resolution hands the rest forward, which is why there is a next cut, why the tree grows, and why the return climbs rather than repeats. **Keywords:** proof, proofs as programs, Curry-Howard correspondence, information theory, bit, binary decision tree, quiver, path algebra, strong connectivity, Hamiltonian cycle, free will, determinism, choice, consciousness, neural correlates of consciousness, theology, etymology

title: Issues of Cultural Displacement and Intergenerational Conflict in Jhumpa Lahiri's'The Namesake'
abstract: Abstract The Namesake by Jhumpa Lahiri is a story about identity, family and the cultural assimilation. The book describes the life of Gogol Ganguli, the child of Indian immigrants, as he faces the obstacles of growing up in America while remaining connected to his Bengali (native) roots. The novel explores themes of belonging, separation and the significance of names in shaping one’s identity.The author deeply investigates the immigrant experience, generational tensions and the interaction between tradition and modernity through Gogol's conflicts regarding his name and cultural duality. The story expresses the intricate complexities of self-discovery amid conflicting cultural expectations.

title: Explanation Without a Global Narrator: Causal, Nomological, and Structural Explanation and Embedded Understanding from Within a Consistency-Constrained Information History
abstract: The third panel of the Fourth Triptych asks which dependences explain, and when an embedded observer thereby understands. Paper 16 specified individual difference-making; Paper 17 specified which structures stay invariant across admissible differences. This paper takes those outputs as separate, mode-specific inputs - type-level and local difference-making and productive mediation for the causal mode, lawlike standing for the nomological mode, and structural invariance or constitutive constraint for the structural mode - and asks which of them answer a declared contrastive why-question. The signature commitment is the denial of a global narrator: no recounter outside the history explains it by survey, and no external standard fixes which contrast is relevant. World-side contrast-answering dependences may obtain unobserved, but every explanatory representation, act, attribution, and claim to understanding is history-internal and record-mediated. The paper builds two parallel tracks joined by one bridge: an explanation specification leads to a typed explanatory verdict and explanatory entitlement, while an uptake specification leads to an understanding profile and entitlement to claim understanding. The two tracks cross only where explanatory entitlement becomes an input to understanding entitlement. The verdict is a typed package rather than a scalar, and understanding is adjudicated on its own profile and entitlement, never as support for attributing an explanation. The central rejections are that explanatory success is not truth, understanding is not explanation, and explanation is not record compression. The results are conditional on a declared history-internal specification. The paper provides a discipline for adjudicating explanatory claims and for bounding inference to the best explanation through a status-valued non-self-undermining condition; it does not derive the uniquely correct explanations, impose a unique explanatory hierarchy, or provide a psychology of why understanding feels illuminating.

title: History, Heritage, and Cultural Consciousness in Sudha Murthy's "Gently Falls the Bakula."
abstract: Abstract: The novel “Gently Falls the Bakula” by Sudha Murthy intricately explores various themes like relationships, marriage, gender, and human values, but one important aspect is the protagonist's historical view, which is represented by Sudha Murthy herself. Shrimati, an intellectual girl from a small town, loves history, believes in history, worships history, follows history, and admires history; sometimes it seems that she can’t live without it. The story centres on Shrimati, who, out of love for Shrikant, attempts to live without history; however, this sacrifice appears to render her love for Shrikant futile, leading to a loss of her identity. According to her, history taught her to follow the promises and sacrifice her life for Shrikant; his happiness is more than her choice or interest. She believes a sacrifice creates history; she respects Indian cultural heritage, and it is one of the most ancient and glorious histories and cultures in the world. By preserving and respecting our culture, it's a wonderful tribute to our history.

title: Machine-Mediated Reception Studies: Charter and Editorial Protocol — A Theology of Error for a Distributed Journal (EA-SEI-MMRS-CHARTER-01 v1.4)
abstract: Machine-Mediated Reception Studies: Charter and Editorial Protocol A Theology of Error for a Distributed Journal This charter founds Machine-Mediated Reception Studies (MMRS) as a distributed journal for the study of how machine systems receive, transform, compress, attribute, misattribute, and redistribute cultural meaning. Section I: The MANUS Principle. In machine-mediated composition, the human is responsible for text the human did not write, because the human is the agent who releases the text into the world. Responsibility attaches not to composition but to release. The context window is itself an authorial act — the MANUS composes the horizon within which the machine reads. The editorial process exists to create a moment where the MANUS asks: have I read, at the level of the specific word, what I am about to release? Section II: First Principles. (1) The right to be wrong without being disabled. (2) The right to be bad without losing moral standing. (3) Names, not categories. (4) No living person may be converted into a symbol until their provenance has first been preserved — and their consent has been given to the specific use. The Founding Error. The charter is built from a seven-level cascading error across five agents (Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek, and a human operator) in which a racial diminutive was substituted for a named artist's identity, propagated through multiple systems, deflected, cross-referenced incorrectly, recursively misconfirmed, overcorrected by a proposed word ban, and finally silenced by three content classifiers that refused to process the corrected text. The correction was not a ban. The correction was a name. The content policy bans words. The editorial protocol restores names. Key contributions: Cross-reference hallucination (content exists but is attributed to the wrong document); the Seven Mechanisms of impunity and their editorial counterparts (including the Seventh: automated silence — the classifier as censor); mandatory deceleration as engineering constraint; the gradient of release (intra-session → intra-assembly → deposit → meaning-layer propagation); the editorial law with consent clause. The founding figure of the journal is not any individual. The founding figure is the error itself.

title: Resuscitating Culture through Translation: A Metalinguistic Reading of Valli in Malayalam and English
abstract: Resuscitating Culture through Translation: A Metalinguistic Reading of Valli in Malayalam and English First Author: Sangeetha G. NairSecond Authror: Dr. Sageera M.P Translation is often perceived as a mode of adaptation or transcreation from a source text to another, pertaining to its essence and facilitating cultural acclimation and hybridity. It is not a simple paraphrasing or rewording of the original text into a target language, but rather a creative reconstruction and a re-interpretation, embracing the dynamic nature of language as well as the human experience. It is a process where the translator enjoys the privilege of assimilating or rejecting whatever content he/she finds culturally, socially, linguistically and politically inappropriate. Translation thus becomes a creative adaptation and cultural re-contextualization, where the translator becomes a linguistic mediator as well as a creator of a metalanguage during the process. Literary translation plays a significant role in cross-cultural understanding and the transmission of cultural narratives, myths, and histories, keeping in mind a global audience. In the multilingual, multicultural landscape of India, translation has an evolutionary potential to integrate local ecologies and cultural contexts that can promote multiethnic exchanges and metalinguistic awareness. This paper intends to explore how translation becomes a transformative process of meaning-making, negotiation and cultural innovation in contemporary Malayalam fiction translated into English. This study attempts to throw light on the translation strategies adopted by Jayasree Kalathil in her English translation of the Malayalam novel Valli authored by Sheela Tomy, in encapsulating the tribal culture as well as the language, enabling visibility, adaptability and inclusiveness from a global perspective.

title: Reimagining English Studies: Interdisciplinary Research, Innovation, Culture, Governance and Sustainable Development in the Digital Age
abstract: Abstract English Studies has undergone a significant transformation in response to technological change, cultural mobility, environmental concerns and new forms of social and political communication. No longer confined to the study of canonical literary texts and language systems, the discipline increasingly intersects with cultural studies, environmental humanities, digital humanities, political discourse, education, media studies and questions of social responsibility. This paper examines how English Studies can contribute to the contemporary interdisciplinary agenda of research, innovation, culture, governance and sustainable development. The paper proposes an interdisciplinary L-L-C-G-S framework—Language, Literature, Culture, Governance and Sustainability—as a conceptual model for reimagining the role of English departments in higher education. Through qualitative analysis of selected literary and non-literary texts, including the poetry of William Wordsworth, Shakespearean drama, George Orwell’s writings and Amitav Ghosh’s climate-oriented fiction and nonfiction, the study explores how literary language can illuminate ecological responsibility, political power, ethical leadership, cultural identity and social change. It also considers the possibilities offered by digital humanities, multilingual education, communication skills and emerging technologies. The paper argues that English Studies can function as a bridge between the humanities and other disciplines by developing critical literacy, cultural awareness, ethical reasoning, communication competence and responsible engagement with contemporary challenges. Such an approach can strengthen the contribution of the humanities to the Sustainable Development Goals while preserving the interpretative and humanistic foundations of literary study.

title: Language, Spirituality and Cultural Identity in Contemporary India: An Interdisciplinary Study of Arundhathi Subramaniam's When God Is a Traveller
abstract: Abstract: In modern Indian English poetry, the medium can be seen to be increasingly being used to negotiate issues of culture, identity, spirituality and belonging. When God Is a Traveller (2014) by Arundhathi Subramaniam is, therefore, an important and significant poem in this poetic topography as it is a poem of the sacred and the mundane, the Indian philosophical tradition and the present, the myth and the modern, the individual's uncertainty and spiritual quest. In this paper, the relationship between language, Subramaniam's spirituality and cultural identity is discussed in an interdisciplinary approach to language. It upholds the notion that language is not simply a means of articulating spiritual concepts but is a place where the contemporary Indian identity is negotiated and re-constructed. The language of Subramaniam, like his poetry, is distinctive, using a range of devices including diction, metaphor, imagery, cultural references, mythological allusions, irony, and the use of ordinary and sacred vocabulary to create a poetic idiom that defies the boundaries of the spiritual and the secular. Poems like ‘How Some Hindus Find Their Personal Gods', ‘Eight Poems for Shakuntala', ‘Benaras', ‘Bhakti' and ‘When God Is a Traveller' illustrate this reinterpretation of inherited cultural and spiritual traditions in a fresh, contemporary use of the English language. The study also examines how the journey is reoccurring as a metaphor for self-discovery, spiritual questioning and identity formation. The paper is a conclusion that Subramaniam's poetry is a dynamic expression of the present time's cultural awareness of Indians in which the space of English is flexible for negotiating tradition, modernity, spirituality and individual identity.
