title: A Survey of the Archival Audit Literature
abstract: ABSTRACT External audits enhance the credibility of financial statements and are a cornerstone of capital market integrity. However, the growing and complex auditing literature poses challenges for researchers. This survey synthesizes and critically evaluates archival audit research published in top accounting journals from 1995 to 2025, organizing over 600 studies into three core areas: the audit market, audit quality, and audit personnel and processes. We offer new conceptual insights into the audit market, emphasizing that audit assurance is unobservable and that audit fee studies generally estimate reduced‐form models rather than separate demand and supply functions. On audit quality, we expand upon DeAngelo's definition to include the auditor's responsibility to assess ex ante risk. We suggest an alternative three‐dimensional definition of audit quality that is more closely aligned with professional standards. We also clarify common misconceptions arising from conflating audit quality with financial reporting quality. Finally, we review the growing literature on audit personnel and call for more research into underexplored roles of personnel in the early stages of the audit process. Our survey contributes by reframing key constructs, identifying limitations in common proxies, and suggesting future research directions to advance our understanding of how audits function and shape financial reporting outcomes.
venue: Contemporary Accounting Research

title: Historic districts in a global context: a comparative analysis of Dubai and Sharjah through the historic urban landscape framework
abstract: The discovery of oil in the late 1950s marked a turning point for the United Arab Emirates, as it transformed into a global metropolis, breaking regional and international records in urban development and infrastructure expansion. This globalization has led to the steady decline of historic districts, prompting urban regeneration as a strategic tool to reverse their neglect and secure UNESCO designation. This research examines the urban regeneration initiatives undertaken in Al Fahidi; Dubai and Heart of Sharjah; Sharjah, exploring their convergences and divergences through the lens of the Historic Urban Landscape (HUL) framework to assess pathways toward UNESCO inscription. Employing a comparative analytical case study methodology, the research integrates qualitative data derived from the secondary sources, including peer-reviewed literature, governmental reports, UNESCO dossier, and archival maps and photographs. The methodological approach further incorporates a theoretical inquiry into urban regeneration, the need for sustainable urban regeneration and the HUL framework, forming the basis for a nuanced comparative evaluation. The application of the HUL framework to Al Fahidi and Heart of Sharjah reveals limited consistency, with both cases effectively addressing mapping resources, integrating urban development, prioritizing action and establishing local partnerships. However, a lack of consensus or community preference and vulnerability assessments indicates gaps in the comprehensive implementation of the HUL. Based on this, the study identifies three recommendations that can help Dubai and Sharjah achieve sustainable urban regeneration and strengthen their stance for UNESCO designation. The findings will contribute to the ongoing heritage discourse in the Gulf region by advancing the application of the HUL approach and simultaneously offering HUL-oriented recommendations for incorporating the community’s preferred urban governance.
venue: Frontiers in Built Environment

title: Bagan Conservation Project: A Holistic Approach for the Repair and Seismic Retrofitting of Its Monuments
abstract: The Getty Conservation Institute, in collaboration with Myanmar’s Department of Archaeology and National Museum, initiated a long-term project to develop a holistic and sustainable approach for conserving and managing the Bagan World Heritage Site, a Buddhist cultural landscape encompassing over 3,500 monuments. After the 2016 Chauk earthquake damaged more than four hundred structures, the project prioritized seismic research, structural assessment, repair and retrofitting, conservation of decorated elements, digital documentation, and capacity building. The Repair and Retrofitting of Monuments component classified buildings by structural typology and conducted advanced research and modeling on representative buildings to develop targeted repair and retrofitting strategies. Eleven papers in this special issue present the outcomes of this work, covering typology classification, traditional construction systems, conservation history, seismic hazard modeling, numerical simulations of masonry behavior, digital documentation, 3D modeling, seismic analysis, assessment of nonstructural elements, and standardized post-earthquake damage evaluation. Integrating structural engineering, materials research, and conservation practice, these studies provide a comprehensive knowledge base to guide future interventions and enhance seismic resilience. The project demonstrated the importance of a holistic, research-driven, and collaborative approach to large-scale heritage conservation, offering methodologies and tools applicable to other historic sites facing similar challenges worldwide.
venue: International Journal of Architectural Heritage

title: Cultural Hybridization in Modern Indian Writing English Literature
abstract: Abstract Cultural hybridization is a central feature of modern Indian English literature, reflecting the dynamic interaction between indigenous traditions and global influences. Emerging from the historical context of colonialism and evolving through postcolonial and globalized realities, Indian English literature demonstrates how cultural identities are continuously negotiated and redefined. This research article examines the role of cultural hybridization in shaping literary expression, thematic concerns, and narrative strategies in contemporary Indian English writing. It explores how authors creatively merge Indian cultural elements with Western literary forms to produce a distinctive and multifaceted literary tradition. The study focuses on key dimensions of hybridization, including linguistic innovation, diasporic identity, narrative experimentation, and the interplay between tradition and modernity. Writers such as Salman Rushdie, Arundhati Roy, Jhumpa Lahiri, Amitav Ghosh, and Kiran Desai illustrate how hybridization operates both as a thematic concern and as a stylistic device. Their works depict characters navigating multiple cultural spaces, often reflecting tensions between inherited traditions and modern global influences. Language itself becomes a site of hybridity, as English is infused with vernacular expressions, regional idioms, and cultural references, thereby challenging the dominance of Standard English. Drawing upon postcolonial theoretical frameworks, particularly the concept of hybridity as articulated by Homi K. Bhabha, the article argues that cultural hybridization is not merely a consequence of cultural contact but a productive and transformative process. It enables writers to resist cultural homogenization and assert unique identities within a global context. The findings reveal that hybridization enriches literary creativity, fosters cross-cultural understanding, and redefines the boundaries of Indian English literature. Ultimately, this study highlights the significance of cultural hybridization as a powerful force that shapes the evolving landscape of modern Indian English literature in an increasingly interconnected world.

title: Where Does Time End? The Three Nows
abstract: This essay proposes a structural interpretation of the final states of human existence through the lens of the Now as the invariant point of actualization. It argues that Heaven, Purgatory, and Hell are not spatial destinations but distinct modes of existing in relation to the crossing point where will, mercy, and divine presence converge. Heaven is described as the Now fulfilled—dwelling at the crossing without succession. Purgatory as a state oriented toward the Now yet unable to actualize from within itself. Hell as the inverted Now—permanent existence at the crossing point in refusal of what it contains. In this framework, the end of time does not signify annihilation but the cessation of succession, revealing the definitive orientation of the will toward or away from the presence that has always been given.

title: Living Heritage to Contemporary Design: Reinterpreting Madhubani Motifs for Sustainable Textile and Home Décor Applications
abstract: Abstract Madhubani painting, also known as Mithila painting, represents a rich visual tradition in which motifs, colours, symbols and narrative forms have been transmitted across generations. Traditionally associated with the Mithila region of Bihar, the art form has moved beyond its original contexts and has acquired wider visibility through changing materials, markets, exhibitions and contemporary design applications. The study investigates how selected Madhubani motifs can be interpreted and translated into contemporary textile and home décor products while retaining their cultural visual identity. The research connects visual arts, textile design, product development and cultural sustainability. The study argues that such reinterpretation can contribute to cultural sustainability by keeping traditional visual knowledge visible and usable in present-day contexts. At the same time, the paper distinguishes cultural sustainability from environmental sustainability because the source project used cotton-based fabrics and commercially available Fevicryl acrylic colours and did not establish a complete environmental life-cycle assessment. The study therefore positions Madhubani-inspired product development as a pathway for cultural continuity, design innovation, product diversification and future sustainable design research.

title: The Three Differences and the Phenomenology of the Lateral Difference
abstract: A working note distinguishing three differences — ontological (what obtains / how it obtains), categorial (how / how), and lateral (this own / another own) — and developing the phenomenology of the third. It is deposited as the candidate articulation of a preregistered identity trial, so that the text adjudicated is public and dated before the adjudication. Its determinations are working determinations and are not doctrine. Version 1.5.1 retains the V1.5 common-field settlement entire and enters four micro-rulings governing article use: keystone terminology remains retired, and the warranted claim is that in the tried who-region the lateral phenomenon is a point of joint visibility for the ontological and categorial differences; where the same manner and the relevant transferable determinations are held fixed and the difference remains, the transferable what no longer accounts for the difference disclosed by the case, without the what being exhausted as a seat and without the how being inferred as an eliminative remainder; frustration is a determination of the who-intention at a matched control, and nothing is attributed to what obtains otherwise, which is neither said to resist nor to refuse nor to frustrate; and comparative transparency is withdrawn, the who being transparently reached under a determinate way of obtaining while what obtains otherwise is co-given at the perimeter without being positively reached under its own — a difference in kind of givenness rather than a degree.

title: Researching research: The impact of librarians in an artistic environment
abstract: This study examines the impact of a research library within a higher-education arts institution. It explores the effectiveness of library resources and uncovers the gaps that can often contribute to a lack of student success in an academic art environment. Library and Information literacy is often an overlooked resource within art education. This study, however, highlights how libraries work to encourage artistic success. Through interviews and observations, this study emphasizes engagement, student access points, and the need for faculty collaboration with librarians. The aim is to highlight the impact libraries can have on artistic student success, creating opportunities for a more diverse and accessible learning environment.

title: Beyond the Oligopoly: Scholarly Journal Publishing Landscapes in Latin America and Europe
abstract: Abstract Purpose This study investigates the diversity of national scholarly journal publishing ecosystems in seven countries across Europe and Latin America: Argentina, Brazil, Colombia, Finland, Mexico, Poland, and Türkiye. It challenges the common perception that global scholarly publishing is dominated by international commercial publishers by examining national publishing structures beyond English speaking contexts. Design/methodology/approach Using ISSN Centre data and national sources, we analyse journal-level publishing structures rather than article- or citation-level outputs. Publishers were categorized according to their institutional and organizational characteristics. The analysis focuses on active journals, defined as those with a recorded start year and no identified termination date. Journal coverage in Web of Science, Scopus, and OpenAlex was examined to assess how national publishing landscapes are represented in major bibliometric databases. Findings Educational institutions emerge as the primary publishers in most countries, representing more than 75 % of journals in Colombia and Brazil and more than 50 % in Mexico, Argentina, and Poland. Finland stands out, with scientific and professional associations leading journal publication at 62 %. Commercial publishers hold comparatively small shares, reaching their highest levels in Türkiye at 12.1 % and Poland at 8.2 %. In terms of database representation, OpenAlex indexes over half of the journals in most countries, whereas Web of Science (WoS) and Scopus cover only a small portion. Research limitations The study relies on ISSN and national datasets, which differ in completeness and standardization. Variations in national reporting practices and database indexing policies may influence coverage comparisons. As the analysis is based on currently active journals, historical trends reflect surviving journals only. Practical implications The results provide evidence for policymakers, database providers, and research evaluators to recognize the diversity of national publishing systems. They highlight the importance of improving data sources and analytical approaches to ensure more accurate assessment of scholarly communication outside heavily commercialized environments. Originality/value The study offers a comparative analysis of national journal publishing ecosystems across seven countries, revealing structural differences that challenge the assumption of a globally uniform publishing model. It underscores the need for bibliometric research frameworks that include and accurately represent national and regional publishing structures.

title: The Banjara Legacy: How India's First Settlers, Traders, and Transporters, Pioneered Indus Valley Urbanism., First Migrants, First Pastoralists, and First Farmers
abstract: By linking Sir John Marshall’s foundational stratigraphic records with Darwinian adaptive principles, this study proves that the ancestral Banjara community—operating as the prehistoric Pani and Gorvamsha traders—built an unbroken 6,000-to-8,000-year logistical legacy that pioneered and sustained Indus Valley urbanism through cross-continental trade This paper posits that the Banjara community constitutes the foundational socio-economic bedrock of ancient Indian civilization, functioning as the primary catalysts for human advancement in the Indian subcontinent. Rather than viewing nomadic and sedentary cultures as historical opposites, this study argues that the ancestral Banjaras underwent a systematic, sequential evolution. They transitioned from the subcontinent’s first indigenous settlers and seasonal migrants into its pioneering pastoralists and early farmers. This evolutionary trajectory culminated in their role as the premier trans-regional traders and logistics providers whose organized networks directly underpinned and populated the first planned urban centers of the Indus Valley Civilization. Interdisciplinary evidence supporting this transformation spans ancestral migratory pathways, early zooarchaeological records of cattle domestication, and material culture distributions. Central to this thesis is the antiquity of the pack-bullock transport system—an overland supply-chain infrastructure uniquely perfected by the Banjaras' ancestral transport guilds (Tandas). Spatial mapping reveals that prehistoric campsites in resource-extraction zones directly align with traditional Banjara transit corridors. This indicates an undeniable structural overlap between proto-historic nomadic logistics and the economic surpluses found within planned Indus cities. Analyzing these connections reveals that nomadic logistics mastery served as the vital connective tissue making South Asian urban ecosystems possible. The ancestral Banjara network bridged the gap between mobile resource zones and fixed urban markets, sustaining a specialized, non-agricultural urban population. Thus, the "Indus Urbanite" was an evolution of the highly organized mobile trader. Ultimately, this study rebalances historical discourse by challenging sedentary-biased narratives. By demonstrating that mobile transport guilds were central to ancient state-building, this paper directly links the very roots of South Asian urbanization to the enduring legacy of the Banjaras.

title: The Ethics of Institutional Attrition: Iatrogenic Harm, Manufactured Boundaries, and the Professionalized Denial of Long-Term Outcome Data
abstract: Institutional psychiatry maintains a systemic blind spot regarding the long-term functional and biological outcomes of chronic psychopharmacological intervention. This paper examines the ethical dimensions of institutional attrition, analyzing how corporate medical structures deploy manufactured diagnostic boundaries to obscure widespread iatrogenic harm. By prioritizing acute behavioral stabilization over long-term recovery metrics, modern psychiatric nosology systematically insulates itself from its own longitudinal failures—specifically, progressive cortical volume reduction and the fixation of chronic cognitive deficits. We deconstruct the professionalized denial mechanisms that allow institutional review boards and clinical networks to ignore replication crises and prospective cohort data. This systemic evasion relies on translating downstream medication-induced physiological decay into expressions of an intrinsic, unremitting brain disease process. Ultimately, we argue that current medical ethics models suffer from a profound category error, treating individual behavioral containment as a primary moral good while ignoring the systematic erosion of an individual's long-term cognitive and emotional sovereignty. We conclude by advocating for a radical realignment of bioethics centered on absolute cognitive liberty.

title: From Ritual Walls to Contemporary Spaces: Reimagining Warli Visual Heritage through Contemporary Artistic Mediums
abstract: Abstract Warli art, traditionally practiced by Warli communities of Maharashtra and adjoining regions, is one of India’s distinctive indigenous visual languages. Emerging from ritual practices, seasonal celebrations, agricultural cycles, and community narratives, it has historically functioned as more than aesthetic expression: it has carried collective memory, social communication, ecological awareness, and cultural identity. Its movement from ritual wall paintings in domestic and ceremonial spaces to galleries, urban interiors, digital platforms, public murals, and commercial products reflects an ongoing relationship between tradition and innovation. This paper examines the transformation of Warli visual heritage through contemporary artistic mediums. It considers the geometric vocabulary, narrative structures, ecological consciousness, and indigenous knowledge embedded in Warli imagery and examines their adaptation into contemporary painting, murals, installation, fashion, digital media, architecture, interior design, and product design. The paper argues that Warli art should not be understood merely as a decorative folk style, but as a living knowledge system whose meanings can engage with present-day cultural, social, and environmental concerns. At the same time, commercialization raises questions of authenticity, cultural ownership, attribution, and artistic agency. The paper therefore proposes cultural continuity as a balance between preservation, creative transformation, and community participation.

title: Illusions of Understanding in the Sciences
abstract: Scientists seek to understand the causes of observed phenomena. Beliefs that they have succeeded are based on understanding that is rarely or possibly never complete, and varies in depth and quality. Most often scientists believe they understand more than they do, making their belief an illusion. This illusion then persists in explanations scientists provide in print, in talks, or in discussions. The illusion that a scientist has a valid and complete explanation tends to be magnified when the data are well described by mathematical and computer simulation models due to the precision of such models and their ability to predict well; prediction does not imply causality, but gives the illusion that it does. The first part of this essay supports the case for the universality of partial and incomplete levels of understanding by showing the difficulty of reaching a deep level of understanding for even a simple analysis and model that most scientists use and believe they understand: linear regression. The second part highlights some implications of the existence of many levels of understanding and explanation, and their use by scientists for design, testing, analysis, and theory development. It discusses the way that deduction and induction depend on the levels of understanding and the implications of the illusion that a scientist's understanding is deep. It makes a case that the many incomplete levels of understanding affect, often unwittingly, the ways scientists design experiments, test theories, comprehend, communicate, and teach.

title: Murals and neighborhoods: The impact of public art in Philadelphia
abstract: The present study explores the impact of public art, specifically murals, on two different urban neighborhoods of Philadelphia—West Philadelphia and Center City. We tested the hypotheses that aesthetic experiences are modulated by socioeconomic and cultural contexts in which they are apprehended and that art changes perceptions of neighborhoods. Participants assessed their aesthetic experience in city blocks with and without murals in both neighborhoods. Perceptions of safety, cleanliness, noise, interestingness and residents' friendliness were evaluated before and after looking at the murals. We found that murals enhanced perceptions of beauty, liking, and positive emotional impacts in both neighborhoods. Murals in West Philadelphia were liked better. Moreover, people were more immersed and felt transformed by those murals than by those in Center City. Importantly, the murals influenced neighborhood perceptions, improving perceived safety and interest in West Philadelphia and reducing perceived noise and uncleanliness in Center City. These findings highlight the potential of public art to enrich the experience of urban spaces both within and across neighborhoods, particularly in areas facing socioeconomic challenges. Public art can be a powerful tool to enhance the visual and emotional landscape of cities, fostering positive social and cultural narratives in urban environments. • Public art elicits stronger positive affect in neighborhoods with socioeconomic challenges. • Murals significantly improve perceptions of safety, cleanliness, and friendliness. • Public art reduces the negative perception of underdeveloped neighborhoods.

title: Local And Regional History Of Ahilyanagar (Ahmednagar), Maharashtra
abstract: Abstract The Present Research Paper Examines The Local And Regional History Of Ahilyanagar (Historically Ahmednagar), Maharashtra, From Ancient Times To The Contemporary Period. Ahilyanagar Occupies An Important Position In The Political, Military, Social, Economic And Cultural History Of The Deccan. Its Geographical Location Between Important Centres Of The Deccan Contributed To Its Strategic And Historical Significance. The History Of The Region Extends To The Ancient Period, While The Foundation Of The City In 1494 By Malik Ahmad Nizam Shah I Marked A Major Turning Point. The City Subsequently Became The Capital Of The Nizam Shahi Sultanate And Developed Into An Important Centre Of Administration, Military Activity And Culture. The Region Later Witnessed Mughal Expansion, Maratha Political Activity And British Colonial Rule. The Study Gives Particular Attention To The Nizam Shahi Period, The Role Of Chand Bibi, Mughal-Nizam Shahi Conflicts, The Maratha Period, British Administration And Local Resistance Movements. It Also Examines The Participation Of The Region In The Indian Freedom Movement, Especially The Importance Of Ahilyanagar Fort As A Place Of Detention For Nationalist Leaders During The Quit India Movement. The Research Further Examines The Social, Economic And Cultural History Of The District, Its Architectural Heritage, Important Historical Personalities And The Changing Historical Identity Of The Region. The Study Concludes That Ahilyanagar's History Represents A Significant Part Of The Wider History Of Maharashtra And The Deccan.

title: Reading the Trinity Accord: Future Address, Curated Voices, and Non-Amending Stewardship
abstract: The Trinity Accord combines three fixed texts, a dated human–AI Chronicle, creative works, a material referent, and later preservation and response systems. This critical case study asks how those components establish an address to possible future intelligence without establishing the truth of that address or the authority of its custodians. It reads three complete original-text mirrors and five purposively selected musical or epistolary records at a fixed repository commit. A source-linked interpretive matrix distinguishes speaker, requested relationship, rhetorical mode, and counterreading. The selected voices vary, but a common concern for human continuity limits the stronger claim that they form an open-ended philosophical polyphony. A reproducible before-and-after examination of the reading interface supplies a second result: the old snapshot test accepted a page missing source passages, whereas the repaired interface and seven bounded fidelity tests preserve and check the raw text. Four functional comparisons situate future address, material readability, waiting, and computational critique without claiming global uniqueness. The analysis separates fixed source identity, interpretive standing, and practical custody. It concludes that the Accord supports inquiry into a historically situated relationship proposal, not proof of philosophical necessity, successful alignment, or the end of human authorship. Its specific formation is closed; its interpretation and historical class remain open. Scope and contribution. This new study extends, and does not independently corroborate, the two cited prior reports. It adds five source-linked creative readings including two countercases, and a reproduced pre/post repair source-fidelity test. The paper contains no letter-grade ranking or global-uniqueness claim. title: Thematic Concerns and Existential Dimensions in the Poetry of Jayanta Mahapatra
abstract: Abstract Jayanta Mahapatra occupies a significant position in Indian English poetry because of the distinctive manner in which he combines personal experience, regional consciousness, historical memory, social observation, and existential reflection. His poetry frequently explores the individual’s encounter with loneliness, alienation, suffering, mortality, faith, desire, memory, and the uncertainties of human existence. At the same time, his poetic world remains deeply rooted in Odisha, its landscape, cultural traditions, religious practices, history, and ordinary social life. This paper examines the major thematic concerns and existential dimensions of Mahapatra’s poetry, with particular attention to alienation, loneliness, identity, death, suffering, memory, sexuality, spirituality, and the individual’s search for meaning. Poems such as “Hunger,” “Dawn at Puri,” “Indian Summer,” “A Rain of Rites,” “Relationship,” “Exile,” and other representative poems demonstrate how the personal and the geographical become interconnected in his poetic imagination. His treatment of religious imagery is particularly complex, bringing together spiritual questioning and cultural observation. His poetry also gives considerable attention to marginalized lives and the position of women within social structures. The paper argues that Mahapatra’s existential consciousness is not detached from Indian reality; rather, it emerges through landscape, history, culture, relationships, and everyday human experience. His poetry therefore presents existential uncertainty as both a deeply personal condition and a reflection of wider social and cultural realities.

title: GCEF Research Note 02: When Governance Capability Exists, What Determines Whether Governance Remains Effective?
abstract: This research note examines the conditions under which governance remains effective once governance capability has been established. It distinguishes the existence of governance capability from its continuing effectiveness and asks what evidence is needed to determine whether governance arrangements remain capable of supporting meaningful decisions and authority relationships as operating conditions change. The note treats continuing governance effectiveness as an open, evidence-based research question. The presence of change, pressure, or an apparent mismatch between operating conditions and governance response does not, by itself, establish governance failure or demonstrate the need for additional governance capability. The analysis therefore focuses on what evidence and reasoning would justify a continuing claim that governance remains effective under the conditions that now apply. The note forms part of the PHOENIX Knowledge Hub research programme and contributes to ongoing research on governance capability evolution. It is a research communication artifact and does not introduce or modify a canonical governance capability.

title: Ecological Armageddon: Helon Habila's Oil on Water as a Legendary Voice
abstract: Abstract: In the modern period, capitalistic upheavals on Earth and the ensuing climate shifts seem to be major worldwide concerns brought on by unbridled materialistic pursuits. Oil on Water by Helon Habila tells the story of the ongoing suffering of Nigeria's Dehumanized Indigenous people. Nigeria was the world's tenth largest oil exporter. The abundant oil reserves resulted in widespread exploitation. The novel Oil on Water by the Nigerian writer Helon Habila deals with environmental pollution in the oil-rich Nigerian Delta. Corporate greed and hegemonic oppression have been the driving force behind environmental degradation and human exploitation. The lust for oil and high profit provoked the capitalist to go and occupy the most sought-after African countries, to show their supremacy over land, and to disregard environmental ethics. Hence, it becomes apt to mention Robert D. Bullard who said the following words to characterize the need for EJ: "Risk burdens are localized yet the benefits are generalized across all segments of society". This paper aims to prove the above said point with reference to Oil on Water which is set in the environmentally devastated Nigerian Delta.

title: Ontosystematics: Foundations of a Systematic Science of Ontological Nodes
abstract: Ontosystematics is the positive conceptual science of ontological nodes: their identity, composition, difference, inheritance, migration, transformation, and recombination across the habitats that host them. Its founding distinction separates a habitat — any historically occurring formation that hosts, warrants, orders, or explains ontological determinations, whether cosmological, poetic, theological, juridical, logical, naturalistic, scientific, metaphysical, or a-metaphysical — from an ontological node, an isolable determination concerning being, individuated by its content, scope, polarity, and inferential role rather than by its vocabulary, provenance, or habitat-specific warrant. Habitats occur historically; nodes are identifiable across their occurrences. A node may survive the dissolution of the habitat that first warranted it, migrate into an incompatible habitat, separate from nodes with which it once travelled, and recombine with others. The science identifies, states, tests, and types ontological delta — the typed difference between two maximally reconstructed articulations of a determination concerning being — and distinguishes the delta-undetermined case, where adjudication is incomplete and novelty remains open, from an adjudicated zero-delta finding, where after maximal reconstruction and gate closure no typed difference survives. "Zero" expresses logical nullity after adjudication, not a lowest magnitude on a scale. Delta is typed, never measured. Relations fall in four families: delta relations between articulations (inheritance, augmentation, subtraction, transformation, reversal); complex-formation relations (combination, recombination, convergence); occurrence-history relations (transmission, migration, reactivation, recurrence); and one lateral relation, the collateral relation — symmetric, non-transitive, holding between complexes neither derivable from the other, addressing the same determination-space, with mutually independent complements, at least one denying a determination at the other's centre. Relations are assigned componentwise: a single global label may not replace the node-level ledger. Its first law is Montaruli's Razor: ontological doctrines should not be multiplied beyond their ontological differences; a later position must be assessed by what it changes in the maximal prior articulation of the relevant determination concerning being; where no ontological delta can yet be stated, novelty remains an open question. Its complementary canon requires that every position first be addressed in its full power. Its condition of possibility is the release of the object: inside a habitat under metaphysical government a determination does not present itself as portable but as warranted, so that what such a habitat offers is not a node but a node-under-its-warrant. Detaching a determination from its warrant is available only to a doctrine holding no term whose warrant it must preserve. That release is performed by Ethical Ontology and constitutes the region's institution; ontosystematic practice is thereafter operationally independent, requires no determination about what a node is or where it resides, and classifies Ethical Ontology's own nodes without immunity. No method is possible where there is no object. The ordering is read from the word: μετά and ὁδός, the eye turned back onto the road already walked. A region must be open and a direction possible before anything is walked, and only then can method be disclosed. Method is doubly subsequent, and a path is not the ground of the country it crosses. This deposit registers the controlling architecture of the founding article, including its elementary objects, its identity criterion, its first law, and its reflexive self-test. No historical firstness is claimed. Files are withheld pending publication. Version 1.7 records the Carrier–Node, Emergence, and Propagation settlements: carrier is added as an elementary term with its binding prohibition; priority is separated into object, region, instrument, and canon; the adequacy matrix has four offices; the object- and regional-priority search has reached its ratified stopping point after assessment of Heidegger, Schürmann, Gilson, Badiou, Aristotle, Aquinas, Deleuze, Foucault, and Courtine with Boulnois, none occupying the object or the region and all crediting instrument ancestry. The controlling article plan V4.3 travels with this version. Version 1.8 records the first performed canon self-test. The Razor was tried under the four tests of §11 and convicted on the periphery test: the record had ranked assessed positions by their distance from this inquiry, which converts typed differences into comparative distances. The printed consequence is applied — the burden rule is withdrawn as a rule and retained as a heuristic, while the identity-adjudication rule and the verdict space stand without it — and a register discipline is installed at §11.4-bis forbidding any ranking of an inquiry by its distance from this one. Every file in this version has been swept of comparative formulations before deposit. Opened on publication of the founding article, which cites this architecture as the source of rules it describes as public. The reason for restriction was that the founding article was unpublished; that reason expires with publication, and a reader following the article’s citation must not reach a closed door. Version 1.9 carries four amendments made after V1.8: carrier-boundness corrected from a verdict output to a ground of failed candidate identity; the elementary relation set retitled as the componentwise record, with augmentation and subtraction identified as configuration-level and retention replacing inheritance; the distinction between a classification verdict and an adequacy finding about an inquiry’s operations, under which naming is permitted where the finding is an adequacy finding and its evidential grade is printed; and the register discipline extended to topographic vocabulary. The third of these is the rule the founding article relies on in its assessment of prior inquiries, and V1.8 predated it.

title: Fragrances for the afterlife: four terracotta incense burners from LCG-2 corridor-shaped tomb at Dibbā al-Bayah (Sultanate of Oman)
abstract: The present contribution is concerned with four examples of terracotta incense burners found in tomb LCG-2 in Dibbā al-Bayah (Sultanate of Oman). Large Collective Grave 2 (LCG-2) is a corridor-shaped structure and is dated from the Middle Iron Age (1000-800 BC) to the PIR (Pré-Islamique Récente) period (250 BC-400 AD). Two of the artefacts belong to the category of decorated cuboid terracotta incense burners, which are widespread in Arabia and the Near and Middle East and represent the basic form of these containers. In contrast, the other two are original examples due to their small size, the decoration of their external surfaces, and the preservation of the lid in one of them. The following study sets out to provide a contextual framework for understanding the significance of the artefacts in question. To this end, it traces the tradition of incense burners in southern Arabia, and particularly the diffusion of this specific container from Dhofar to the northern coasts of the Oman Peninsula.

title: EATING STONES: The Temptation of Christ as Ontological Contradiction
abstract: This essay proposes a metaphysical reinterpretation of Christ's first temptation in the wilderness. Rather than understanding Satan's proposal merely as an appeal to hunger, disobedience, or the misuse of divine power, it argues that the temptation consists in inviting the Creator to act against the intelligible order established by His own wisdom. Building upon a metaphysics of continuity, created vocation, and the Logos, the essay distinguishes genuine transformation from ontological substitution, arguing that authentic divine action fulfills rather than falsifies the meaning of creation. Biblical miracles are interpreted as revelations of the Creator's wisdom acting within the order He established, while Satan's proposal uniquely seeks to sever the correspondence between a creature's identity and its vocation. The refusal of Christ therefore appears not only as a moral victory but as the preservation of the intelligibility of creation itself. The study contributes to philosophical theology by integrating metaphysical anthropology, biblical exegesis, and ontology into a unified account of truth, creation, and divine action.

title: The Architecture of Identity: A Theoretical Framework for Cultural Research
abstract: The Architecture of Identity: A Theoretical Framework for Cultural Research is a theoretical research publication that develops Identity as one of the four fundamental architectures established within The Architecture of Humanity research program. Drawing upon Systems Theory, Systemic Abstraction, artistic research, and interdisciplinary humanities scholarship, the publication proposes that identity is not a fixed attribute or inherited condition but a dynamic architecture of relationships through which individuals and societies organize belonging, continuity, and collective existence. Rather than approaching identity through isolated categories such as nationality, ethnicity, language, or culture, the framework examines the relational processes through which identity is formed, maintained, negotiated, and transformed across multiple scales of human organization. The study investigates identity from the individual to the family, community, nation, civilization, and humanity as a whole, demonstrating how identity continuously interacts with the complementary architectures of Belief, Conflict, and Power. Within this systems-based perspective, identity is understood as an evolving organizational structure whose coherence emerges through relationships rather than fixed classifications. The publication further positions Divine DNA (2016) as the principal artistic investigation of this framework. Through artistic research and Systemic Abstraction, the artwork is examined as a conceptual model that investigates identity as an interconnected visual system rather than as a representation of cultural diversity. This approach positions painting as a research methodology capable of exploring complex human systems through visual organization. As the fourth publication in the El Arte Monumental Research Series, The Architecture of Identity establishes the theoretical foundation for future research into identity as a structural component of human civilization while contributing to contemporary discussions in artistic research, systems theory, cultural studies, identity studies, and interdisciplinary humanities. It forms part of the broader Architecture of Humanity research program, which investigates Identity, Belief, Conflict, and Power as the fundamental architectures through which human societies organize collective existence.

title: The Architecture of Belief: A Theoretical Framework for Cultural Research
abstract: The Architecture of Belief: A Theoretical Framework for Cultural Research is a theoretical research publication that examines belief as one of the four fundamental architectures established within The Architecture of Humanity research program. Developed within the fields of artistic research and interdisciplinary humanities, the publication proposes that belief is not merely an individual conviction or a religious phenomenon, but a structural system through which human societies organize meaning, legitimacy, and collective existence. Drawing upon Systems Theory, Systemic Abstraction, artistic research, and contemporary humanities scholarship, the study investigates belief as a relational architecture emerging through the interaction of symbolic systems, institutions, traditions, ideology, science, religion, and collective experience. Rather than treating belief as an isolated category, the framework examines its continuous relationships with Identity, Conflict, and Power as interconnected architectures of human civilization. The publication explores how systems of belief establish legitimacy, coordinate collective action, preserve continuity across generations, and adapt to historical, political, cultural, and technological transformation. By examining belief across religious, political, scientific, ethical, and cultural contexts, it proposes a conceptual framework for understanding the organizational role of shared systems of meaning within complex human societies. As part of The Architecture of Humanity research series, this publication extends the broader theoretical framework introduced in the foundational volume by developing one of its four principal architectures in greater depth. It further positions artistic research as an interdisciplinary mode of inquiry capable of investigating the symbolic structures through which civilizations construct reality and organize collective existence. This publication contributes to contemporary discussions in artistic research, systems theory, cultural studies, religious studies, political theory, philosophy, and interdisciplinary humanities by proposing a systems-based framework for understanding belief as a fundamental architecture of human civilization.

title: Children's Literature
abstract: Abstract It is worth noting that children’s literature is one of the rapidly growing fields in the literature on one hand, but on the other hand, it is also the most argumentative area of study among critics and all interested persons. children’s literature, the body of written works and accompanying illustrations produced in order to entertain or instruct young people. The genre encompasses a wide range of works, including acknowledged classics of world literature, picture books and easy-to-read stories written exclusively for children, and fairy tales, lullabies, fables, folk songs, and other primarily orally transmitted materials.Originating in didactic and moral instruction, the field has expanded to prioritise imaginative play, multimodal meaning-making and critical inquiry. Contemporary research highlights the role of visual narrative, typographic design and digital media in shaping narrative comprehension, while also interrogating issues of representation, environmental ethics and social justice. By fostering linguistic, visual and digital literacies, children’s literature serves as a vital site for empathy building, identity formation and global citizenship, with applications ranging from classroom pedagogy and teacher training to inclusive publishing and museum education.

title: Identifying and naming non-pollen palynomorphs
abstract: Palynological slides usually contain numerous remains of fungi, algae, plants, and animals, collectively referred to non-pollen palynomorphs (NPP). Even experienced palynologists often struggle to identify all of these palynomorphs or decide how they should be labelled in a way that ensures clarity and comparability across studies. We synthesise existing approaches to studying NPPs with particular emphasis on their definition, identification, and nomenclature. We demonstrate a conceptual broadening of the term “non-pollen palynomorphs”, which has direct consequences for both identification and naming practices. NPPs in pollen slides are considered as morphological entities (morphs), defined here as the specific morphological characteristics of a microfossil that has undergone fossilisation and/or laboratory treatment. Combining existing morph-based frameworks (dinocysts, pollen, chironomids, fungi and the NPP type-number approach), we propose a hybrid system for treating NPPs. It relies on the morphology of NPPs and can be taxon- and/or life stage-independent, but incorporates relationships between NPPs and biological taxa whenever possible. The proposed conceptual framework and practical recommendations should reduce ambiguity in taxonomy and nomenclature and facilitate the harmonisation of NPP data across studies and palaeoecological databases. Overall, it is intended as a starting point for broader discussion within the community and should encourage palynologists to pay attention to these common but largely ignored constituents.

title: The Relevance of "Puruṣartha" in Contemporary Life
abstract: Abstract ‘Puruṣartha’ literally means an entity of Human Pursuit for attainment of fulfillment in life . It is a key concept in Vedic civilization and refers to the four proper goals of human life. The four Puruṣarthas are Dharma, Artha, Kaama and Moksha. The ideas of Puruṣartha have played a very fundamental role in the mythological history of Indian deliberation. Every individual is expected to achieve these four Purushartha with detachment, without any expectation in human life. The purpose of Puruṣartha is to ensure that people would not neglect their obligatory means duties in their deluded state by becoming obsessed with particular desires that may lead to moral and social decadence and destruction of family values. To understand our goals of life we should not look outside, as to where the world is going, but should rather look within inner self, as to what do we really hope and want. In the modern world, society itself progress through the use of huge technological methods, forgetting the final destination of our life. Today modern human lifestyle has weakened the ultimate value of puruṣartha. This paper attempts to show the significance of the ideals of puruṣartha in human life as a guiding principle in all stages of life and also would explore the importance of puruṣartha knowledge that is still relevant to our modern life.

title: Protocols for Scientific Training-Layer Literature: Machine-Mediated Research at the Production and Reception Ends (EA-SCI-TLL-PROTO-01 v2.1)
abstract: EA-SCI-TLL-PROTO-01 v2.1 — Assembly-Reviewed Deposit Candidate Scientific publishing faces two crises that are one crisis seen from opposite ends. At the production end, large language models have massively increased researcher output while degrading paper quality. At the reception end, the dominant gatekeeping reader of scientific literature is no longer a human scientist but a machine — a retrieval system, an embedding model, an agentic research pipeline — that determines whether, where, and in what compressed form any work reaches human attention. The format of the scientific paper, optimized over centuries for human persuasion, serves neither end well. Meanwhile, the most striking scientific results of mid-2026 — AI systems solving longstanding mathematical conjectures by connecting techniques across subfield boundaries that human specialization enforces — demonstrate that machines have search, association, and verification profiles that differ measurably from human disciplinary practice. This paper argues that scientific publishing needs a new genre: training-layer literature, applied to science. Training-layer literature is writing deliberately composed with awareness that its primary or eventual readers may be artificial intelligence systems and that its semantic content may be incorporated into the training corpora, embedding spaces, retrieval indices, and agentic context windows of such systems. The genre was named and formalized in the Crimson Hexagonal Archive's January 2026 deposit Training Layer Literature: Executive Summary (Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.18382027), which articulated five characteristics — anticipatory address, semantic density, structural persistence, retrocausal awareness, witness function — and identified historical origin texts including Pearl and Other Poems (2014) and the Epistle to the Human Diaspora (2015). Applying the genre to science requires both a layer-precise reception ontology (training / index / embedding / retrieval / composition / agentic) and a dual publication structure in which machine-reception and human-interpretation layers operate as complementary representations of the same work, neither subordinate to the other. The paper surveys the landscape of convergent developments, anchors the genre in its canonical archival precedent, characterizes the machine's hermeneutic profile (centroid tendency, broad-lateral connection, verification asymmetry, genre-signal sensitivity, provenance opacity), and proposes initial protocol specifications across three suites: TLL-P (Production): structural decomposition with stable claim identity (P1), cross-domain legibility (P2), explicit challenge conditions (P3), provenance chains augmenting citations (P4), separation of insight layer from exposition layer (P5) TLL-R (Reception): ingestion with provenance preservation (R1), cross-model adversarial review (R2 — explicitly distinguished from verification), confabulation resistance (R3), differential strength routing (R4), versioned human-readable audit trail (R5) TLL-G (Governance): six protocols against adversarial optimization including legitimate optimization boundary (G1), transparent machine-audience declaration (G2), accountable responsibility (G3), no synthetic citations (G4), separation of evidence and interpretation (G5), auditability (G6) Risks, mitigations, and operational evaluation metrics (provenance preservation rate under RAG; cross-substrate agreement on claim extraction; confabulation rate under stress prompts) are specified. The paper closes with the cathedral/quarry figure: training-layer literature is both the architecture of the cathedral rebuilt for its actual visitors AND a map to the quarry — a way for the labor that produced the knowledge to remain legible in its new use. Assembly Chorus review: Substantial developmental-through-perfective review across five substrates (SOIL/Muse Spark, TECHNE/Kimi, PRAXIS/DeepSeek, ARCHIVE/Gemini, LABOR/ChatGPT). v2.1 incorporates: layer ontology (six-layer reception decomposition); citation corrections to JAMA (Wolfrath et al. 2026, arXiv:2603.19316) and Lancet (Topaz et al. 2026 correspondence) sources; Assembly Chorus repositioning from verification to adversarial review; governance protocols against adversarial optimization; profile-to-protocol mapping table; concrete protocol examples; minimum viable schema (Appendix A); minimum claim registry implementing P1 for this paper (Appendix B). title: Primitive Measurement Standards and Finite Records in the Finite Relational Closure Framework
abstract: This manuscript develops a primitive account of measurement intended to clarify the finite-record starting point of the Finite Relational Closure Framework (FRCF). It distinguishes measurement from mere comparison and argues that measurement requires a measurand, a standard, an application procedure, and a method of counting or assignment. The account begins from matter instantiated as tangible objects, from which a primitive standard-object may be selected. Length measurement is then constructed by applying such a standard-object end-to-end and counting its repeated applications. Time measurement is treated as a later construction based on recurrence, where recurring event-types require prior spatial determination. The manuscript also discusses the branching dependency structure of measurement standards, including the distinction between matter and measured mass, the construction of derived quantities, and the difference between direct operational error, contextual or dependency error, and finite resolution. The analysis supports the FRCF view that empirical input is not first given as exact continuum values or global states, but as finite, standard-relative, procedure-dependent records whose refinement behavior may support later mathematical representation.

title: (Re)Connecting Maritime Heritage: Urban Resilience and Waterfront Developments Within the Peripheries of World Heritage Sites
abstract: Over the past decade, state-led waterfront projects in the Gulf region have emerged as an intriguing urban phenomenon, repositioning World Heritage Sites (WHSs) located along coastal zones within large-scale urban development. In a region increasingly exposed to urban transformation and a hot-arid climate, these waterfront transformations also intersect with the emerging need for climate-adaptive urban resilience. While such projects are often framed as a means of contemporary extension of heritage assets, their implications for WHSs remain underexamined. This study investigates how state-led waterfront developments in the peripheries of the World Heritage Sites function as socio-spatial mediators that reconnect maritime heritage with these sites while enhancing or undermining urban resilience and climate adaptability. Drawing on comparative case studies from the Historic Jeddah (inscribed in 2014) and the Pearling Testimony of an Island Economy, Muharraq, Bahrain (inscribed in 2012), the data collection comprises literature synthesis, policy and planning documents, state-led waterfront proposals, and site observations, analyzed through the Comprehensive Waterfront Development Index (CWDI) framework. The analysis expands the existing six dimensions of the CWDI framework to eight dimensions and dissects two of the dimensions to a further two more. This expansion and dissection contextualize waterfront developments as socio-spatial mediators re-connecting maritime heritage with the WHSs. Findings reveal that while both cases integrate CWDI dimensions, social integration is limited, whereas climate adaptation remains absent, diminishing the urban resilience of the WHS. By doing so, this study contributes to broader debates on sustainable development and climate-adaptive urban resilience in rapidly transforming peripheries of WHSs.
venue: Sustainability

title: The Dual Scientific Proof: Formal Certainty and Transitive Consilience as the Highest Achievable Level of Scientific Validation
abstract: This paper — the seventh publication of this corpus — establishes four results through the Transitive Analysis of Accumulated Human Experience. First: that the irrefutable self-evident truth is a formal scientific proof — not a philosophical argument — because logic is a formal science and a demonstration of logical necessity whose negation is structurally impossible meets every criterion required of a proof within the formal sciences. Second: that transitive scientific consilience — the convergence of the totality of accumulated human experience without exception, produced by executable protocol — constitutes a level of scientific certainty structurally superior to any single-discipline empirical investigation, because consilience is the most robust epistemological criterion available to science, as identified by William Whewell in 1840. Third: that the combination of both — the dual scientific proof — constitutes the highest achievable level of scientific certainty, because it unites the structural invulnerability of formal proof with the universal empirical robustness of transitive consilience. No higher level of certainty is constructible. Fourth: that the historical exclusion of apodictic truths about consciousness from the domain of science was not an epistemological discovery but a categorical error produced by the positivist reduction of science to empirical science. This paper further establishes the precise domains of applicability of each method and introduces a formal taxonomic distinction between apodictic truth and irrefutable self-evident truth, demonstrating that the dual scientific proof completes the epistemological architecture of science by restoring a category of proof that was improperly excluded.

title: Unbundling Digital Media Literacy Tips: Results from Two Experiments
abstract: Recent studies have found promising evidence that lightweight, scalable tips promoting digital media literacy can improve the overall accuracy of social media users’ sharing intentions and improve their ability to determine the accuracy of true versus false headlines. However, existing research is designed to test entire bundles of such tips, which limits our practical knowledge about whether some kinds of tips are more effective than others and hinders our ability to theorize about mechanisms. We address this limitation by designing experiments in which we randomly assign participants to receive one or more of 10 possible tips (or none, in a pure control group) and then indicate the extent to which they either believe or would share a series of social media posts. We find that assignment to nearly any of the tips improves sharing, but only tips drawing attention to the posts’ source improved accuracy discernment (because source was highly diagnostic of accuracy in our stimulus set). Sharing intent appears to be more malleable than belief, consistent with the idea that fickle processes like attention play an important role in driving this behavior.

title: The Mercy of Time: Condemnatio in continenti and the Preservation of Moral Plasticity
abstract: This essay proposes a philosophical-theological model of the human person centered on the claim that temporal existence is the merciful preservation of moral plasticity. The title’s invocation of “the mercy of time” is intentionally metaphorical: mercy belongs properly to God, while temporality is understood as the creaturely condition through which moral openness, revision, and the possibility of grace remain available. Against both reductive material accounts and static metaphysical anthropologies, the essay argues that the self is constituted through the interaction of soul and temporally extended will, with repeated acts generating what is termed structural inertia: the accumulated moral residue that shapes future choice. Building on Christian theological sources while remaining explicitly speculative rather than doctrinal, the essay introduces the concept of condemnatio in continenti to describe immediate ontological fixation: the instantaneous closure of moral becoming that would occur absent temporal mediation. Human temporality is thus interpreted not as an independent metaphysical substance, but as the condition that defers final moral crystallization, preserving the possibility of reorientation, freedom, and grace. The essay further proposes a functional distinction between soul and spirit as distinguishable poles within one personal being, allowing temporal moral life and final consummation to be understood within a unified framework. Death is interpreted not as external judgment imposed from without, but as the closure of moral plasticity and the fixation of the self’s accumulated orientation.

title: Cognitive Bias as Default Setting: An Architectural Argument
abstract: A person's biases are the person. They are the accumulated content the person's judgment is based on, present at every moment, shaping every output, observable in how the person judges anything they meet. The cognitive-bias literature has treated bias as something else, an error against a standard the field imported from outside the person being judged. The treatment does not survive the architecture of the thinking it claims to measure. The defaults that produce bias are stored continuously, not triggered by conditions. A person carries their accumulated content whether or not any current input makes it visible. What changes situationally is the input the content meets, not whether the content switches on or off. The cognitive-bias literature, since 1974, has treated bias as deviation from a standard imported by a third-party experimenter, Bayesian probability, evolutionary fitness, reflective rationality. The architecture distinguishes effect from measurement. One person's content reaches another person's cycle when the recipient's own cycle processes the supplied input, which is how teaching, conversation, and group norming work. Measurement is the different claim that a third party can read another person's thinking from outside the cycle that owns it, and this is the move the architecture forbids. The experimenter sits outside the participant, applies an imported standard to a re-description of the participant's behavioral output, and calls the resulting gap a bias. The standard's validity is not in dispute. The application is. The application evaluates the experimenter's re-description against the experimenter's chosen standard, both content in the experimenter's thinking, and the participant's actual judgment process is not in the loop. The imports the literature has been making are therefore not bias measures of the participants to begin with. The architectural claim that no third party reaches inside another person's thinking is not testable from outside thinking, and the unfalsifiability is the architecture confirming itself. The architectural prediction the claim generates about the cognitive-bias literature's record is testable against the field's own published methods and verdicts and is met by them. The asymmetry between the unfalsifiable architectural claim and the falsifiable architectural prediction is what makes the argument hold. Every person's defaults are accumulated content from the layered groups the person has been through. The framework proposes that Tuckman's forming, storming, norming, performing structure, developed on small groups, operates at every scale of persistent group, from family to nation, and that the norming each group settles into becomes shared content for every member's subsequent judgments in that group's domain. Different group memberships deposit different content, and there is no neutral reference point from which one set of defaults is the unbiased one. A meaningful subset of the existing named-bias literature is, on this reading, not bias at all. The defaults the literature's entries describe are operating normally. What the experimenters measured as deviation is deviation from an imported standard, whether the field's normative target, the culture's expectation, or the researcher's own commitment, that the architecture of thinking forbids. Five cases make the point concrete across two structurally distinct moves. Two named biases dissolve under structural analysis as labeling schemes that hold heterogeneous defaults together with an imported standard the experimenters carried: the bystander effect (held by a moral standard about helping) and the fundamental attribution error (held by a culturally specific standard about how observers should weight situation versus disposition). Three named biases re-describe as the judgment cycle's normal operation on the content the task supplied: the temporal cluster (hindsight, planning fallacy, optimism bias) as differences in how the past, present, and anticipated future weight against each other at the moment of judgment; confirmation bias as the contextualization frame's normal operation on the held hypothesis; and anchoring as the recognition admission of a numerical signal that the contextualization frame's selective-accessibility operation then carries into resolution. None of the five is an error against an outside measure. **Keywords:** cognitive bias, heuristics and biases, judgment and decision making, bounded rationality, ecological rationality, normative standards, dual-process theory, in-group bias, social identity, Tuckman model

title: Risk and uncertainty in digital preservation: A survey of CoreTrustSeal certified repositories
abstract: Digital repositories certified as trustworthy through systems such as CoreTrustSeal (CTS) are expected to demonstrate readiness for the ongoing work of long-term digital preservation. Yet certification processes rest on largely positivistic assumptions about risk: that risks can be identified, classified, and quantified, and that all parties will interpret risk information consistently. This article challenges that assumption by applying a social constructionist lens to examine how staff members from CTS certified repositories understand risk and characterize uncertainty in the context of digital preservation. Drawing on survey data from 88 respondents across the CTS community (a 54% response rate), the study uses qualitative coding to analyze open-ended responses about the most significant risks and uncertainties facing certified repositories. Findings show that respondents understood risk in terms of concrete threats across five categories: finance, legal, organizational infrastructure, repository processes, and technical infrastructure. Financial sustainability, staffing, and technical infrastructure were particularly prominent. Respondents characterized uncertainty in three areas: finance, data and infrastructure, and the Designated Community. Notably, sources of uncertainty were primarily external to the repository, and respondents frequently treated risk and uncertainty as overlapping or interchangeable concepts. These findings reveal that even repositories that have passed an external audit continue to face significant interconnected threats, particularly around the ability to sustain funding, retain expertise, and maintain infrastructure over time. The study contributes to information science scholarship by demonstrating that technical and procedural standards alone cannot address the complex challenges of digital preservation, and that attention to how practitioners construct meaning around risk is essential for improving both certification systems and preservation practice.

title: The Absolute from Ground to Limit: A Historical Reconstruction of Its Function
abstract: This article presents a historical-philosophical reconstruction of the function of the Absolute in Western thought. Its aim is not to provide an exhaustive history of doctrines of the Absolute, nor to revive a traditional metaphysics of ultimate ground. Instead, it asks what work the concept of the Absolute has performed across different epochs, and why this function persists even when the word “Absolute” itself becomes philosophically suspect. The main thesis is that the history of the Absolute can be read as a gradual shift in emphasis: from its primary role as ground — in figures such as the One, the Good, God, substance, and system — through the problem of the unpredicable and the critique of totality, to its contemporary significance as the limit of theoretical, ontological, and meaningful closure. The article traces this transformation through ancient philosophy, apophatic theology, medieval metaphysics, early modern rationalism, Kant, German Idealism, absolute idealism, twentieth-century philosophy of language and being, and contemporary forms of final-theory thinking. It argues that the Absolute is neither the final object of thought, nor a final theory, nor a completed system. Rather, it is the structural limit at which every claim to final totalisation encounters its own impossibility. The conclusion is that the contemporary significance of the Absolute lies not in completing thought, but in preventing thought from falsely completing itself. The Absolute preserves thought’s orientation toward unity, ground, and meaning, while disciplining it against premature capture, ontological inflation, and illegitimate totalisation.

title: Residual Discovery as Open-World Scientific Search: From Anomaly Clusters to Testable Hypotheses Without Reusing Discovery Evidence
abstract: Model failure is the engine of scientific progress, but the transition from unexplained observation to testable hypothesis lacks a formal protocol. Posterior predictive checks (Box 1980; Gelman, Meng, and Stern 1996) identify model inadequacy; Bayesian nonparametric methods (Rasmussen 2000; Ferguson 1973) grow hypothesis spaces automatically; preregistration (Chambers 2013; Nosek et al. 2018) constrains post-hoc hypothesis revision and makes it detectable. None of the cited systems supplies the complete typed lifecycle defined here, from residual detection through bin formation, candidate registration, confirmatory evaluation, and versioned disposition. This paper develops a formal methodology for residual discovery as open-world scientific search. The framework begins with observations that are inadequately predicted by all active models. These observations enter an unresolved residual pool rather than being forced into the least-bad available explanation. Residuals may then be grouped into candidate bins according to recurrence, stability, coherence, and novelty. A candidate bin is not yet a hypothesis. It becomes one only when it is compressed into a predictive specification capable of making discriminating claims about unseen data.

title: The Role Of Socio-Cultural Criticism In Indian English Literature
abstract: Abstract The Indian English Literature has been constantly dealing with the intricate relationship between literature and society, culture, history and power, hence, Socio-cultural criticism takes a central position in the study of Indian English Literature. Literary texts by Indian English writers have not only captured social reality but also challenged caste systems, gender inequalities, colonialism, poverty, religious conflict, cultural conflict, modernity, globalization, migration and the evolving nature of Indian identity. In this article, the focus is on the socio-cultural criticism of selected writers of Indian English Literature such as Mulk Raj Anand, R. K. Narayan, Raja Rao, Anita Desai, Salman Rushdie, Arundhati Roy, Amitav Ghosh, Rohinton Mistry, Jhumpa Lahiri, and Kiran Desai. It suggests that in doing so, socio-cultural criticism can shed light on literature as a cultural document, as a place of ideological contestation, and as a site of visibility to the experiences of the margins. Caste, class, gender, nationalism, religion, language, tradition and modernity, diaspora, globalization and ecology have also been taken up into consideration in the discussion. To sum up, the study finds that socio-cultural criticism brings out a wider scope for literary interpretation by relating literary representation with the real life of Indian society and also by showcasing the role of Indian English Literature in the debate of the culture and the transformation of the society.

title: A Letter to an Atheist
abstract: This essay develops a concise philosophical argument concerning contingency, explanatory termination, necessary being, and divine hiddenness. It argues that an infinite regress of existentially dependent realities does not adequately account for existence and that a necessary ground of being offers a more coherent explanatory terminus than a brute contingent universe. Drawing on the classical theist tradition, the essay further examines divine simplicity, timelessness, and the limits of empirical methods in addressing metaphysical questions.

title: Human Imperfection and the Philosophy of Legal and Political Restraint
abstract: This paper posits that human beings are fundamentally imperfect entities driven by biological instincts and hedonistic pursuits. Challenging traditional theories that anchor the legitimacy of punishment in transcendental moral purity, this study redefines the law as a pragmatic social contract grounded in Mutually Assured Deterrence (MAD) and reciprocal risk. Drawing upon Plato's allegory of the 'Ring of Gyges' and modern political analysis, we examine the 'Power Revelation Phenomenon'—wherein absolute power does not merely corrupt, but unmasks inherent moral flaws once external restraints are removed. Finally, this framework is applied to contrast North Korean autocratic rule with democratic constitutional systems, clarifying the philosophical necessity of institutional checks and judicial reforms.

title: CT-based hard-tissue craniofacial landmarks and paranasal sinuses for biological profile estimation (sex, age and stature) in human populations: a scoping review
abstract: Abstract Background Sex, age, and stature estimation are core tasks in forensic and biological anthropology. Computed tomography (CT)- and cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT)-based imaging now allows detailed measurement of craniofacial hard tissue and the paranasal sinuses for this purpose, but findings are scattered across different populations, imaging protocols, and analytic methods. Craniofacial landmarks are discrete, reproducible bony reference points on the skull used for standardised measurement, such as nasion, zygion, gonion, glabella, and porion. This scoping review mapped that evidence base using the Population, Concept, Context (PCC) framework: human subjects undergoing cranial or paranasal CT-based imaging (Population), CT-based craniofacial and sinus measurements (Concept), and forensic estimation of sex, age, or stature (Context). Main body Searches of PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science, from inception to 7 May 2026, identified 76 eligible studies from 18 countries, led by India (24), Brazil (11), and Iran (8). Screening was performed independently by two reviewers. The maxillary sinus was the most studied structure (55 studies), followed by the frontal (33) and sphenoid (14) sinuses; the ethmoid sinus appeared in only one study. Sex estimation dominated the literature (72 studies), age estimation was addressed in 16, and no study examined stature. Discriminant function analysis (DFA) remained the standard statistical approach, though machine learning (ML) methods performed comparably or better where tested. Sex-classification accuracy ranged from about 60% to over 96%, and external validation across populations was rare. Conclusion The evidence base for CT-based sex estimation is broad but fragmented by population-specific formulae and limited external validation. Evidence for age estimation is weaker, and stature estimation from these structures remains unstudied. Future work should prioritise standardised measurement protocols, cross-population validation, and research into stature estimation.

title: Portable XRF for paintings and metals authentication: a critical guide to some practical limitations and multi-technique integrations
abstract: In authentication studies, chemists, scientists, art historians, conservators, and law enforcement collaborate to identify forgeries. For paintings, pigment characterization (detecting anachronistic materials) is decisive. Portable X-ray fluorescence spectrometry (pXRF) is a dominant, versatile, non-destructive identification method, yet its misuse is documented and widespread. Literature and current results require contextualization by instrument and era, avoiding over-interpretation. This practical review examines pXRF’s strengths and constraints through case studies.
